Supply
Government's foot intruding into the doors of the newsrooms of the daily newpapers of Canada.
In his very powerful and disturbing novel, "1984", George Orwell wrote about the way in which politicians could corrupt the English language. As well, he dealt with that subject in many of the other pieces he has written. He pointed out that often the most innocuous of terms are used by politicians to throw a veil over the most odious of actions. By co-opting language which was positive, by misusing it, by perverting the language and by making it mean something it was never intended to mean, they were able to mask actions which the public at large would refuse to accept if they were honestly presented.
a (1250)
Nowhere could there be a better example of what Orwell was referring to than for a Government, under the guise of legislation dealing with freedom of the press, ostensibly to enhance freedom of the press, to bring in measures which would make the press financially beholden to that Government, make it so that potential purchasers of news outlets would have to win the favour of the Government before they could act, and make the actions of working journalists subject to scrutiny and review by a government-sponsored and, in large part, government-appointed press council. What could be more dangerous than that? What could be a worse corruption of language than that which, in its face, seems straightforward? If Orwell were here today I think he would be amazed to find how well the Government has learned the techniques he warned about in passage after passage.
If we are to preserve the freedoms of Canadians, it is essential that we begin now to prevent any action by the Government which will chip away, erode, undermine or circumscribe those fundamental freedoms.
It should be pointed out to the Government that it is ironic that at the very same time as it laments the fact that there are fewer daily newspapers in Canada, it has made no positive proposals that would increase the number of dailies. It has not suggested changes to tax legislation which would encourage advertisers to use the newspapers. It has not proposed changes in legislation that would allow the heirs to independent daily newspapers to be able to hang on when the owner dies and so continue the ownership. Instead of spending money on direct grants to newspapers, the Government has not proposed fellowships for journalists or an increase in funding for journalism schools in the country. These were not concerns of the Government; its concern was the control of a dwindling number of dailies in Canada.
At the same time as the Minister of State for Multicultural-ism complains about the shrinking number of dailies in the country, successive Ministers of Communications have done everything they could to impede the ability of Canadians to see and hear what they would like on their radio and television stations. On the one hand the Government argues that diversity is essential; on the other hand it has consistently tried to prevent that diversity.
Finally, I think I should bring to the attention of the House a statement which perhaps explains better than I can a concern that many people in Canada have about what the Government is doing. When the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts) was Secretary of State, he delivered an address to the 20th General Assembly of UNESCO. He said this:
On every continent there are some people who think that governments should regulate journalists, should tell them, in the public interest, what to write, or should pass judgment on their accuracy. Canadians do not believe that either politicians or public servants should have anything to say in the management, direction or correction of the media. Quite the contrary. In their view, only a free press can guarantee that the decisions of the state power are in harmony with the wishes of the people. Governments have no means of knowing what the needs of society are for its own well being, unless they are told by an informed public.
None of us here today, Mr. Speaker, could have expressed the importance of a free and unfettered press better than did the Minister of the Environment. The onus is on Members here today to take that message to heart and resist attempts by the Government to shackle the free press that is so important to our democracy.

NEW EVALUATION OF FARM LAND SOUGHT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to address a topic of concern which was brought to my attention by the Prince Edward Island Women in Support of Agriculture, regarding farm evaluation. In their annual meeting held on April 13, 1983, the Women in Support of Agriculture passed a resolution which stated:
Whereas farm evaluation has not been revised since 1971, and whereas the rate of inflation, having escalated in the past 12 years, if a farmer sells his farm in 1983 the capital gains tax will be exorbitant, be it resolved that we approach our Members of Parliament and our Members of the Legislative Assembly to request a new evaluation, and by so doing have the capital gains tax lowered.
I support this resolution 100 per cent, Madam Speaker, and feel that capital gains tax should not be assessed to farmers. The policy of the Progressive Conservative Party in the elections of 1979 and 1980 stated that the first $200,000 would not be taxed for capital gains on the sale of a farm.
I join with the P.E.I. Women in Support of Agriculture in urging a new evaluation of farm land, considering how land prices have soared due to inflation since 1971, the last evaluation year. If a farmer sells his land today, his capital gains tax will be exorbitant. I urge that this escalating situation be corrected as the agricultural system is being adversely effected by high property taxes and high capital gains tax. I urge that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) realize the importance of this issue.

subtopic: EMPLOYMENT OF OBSERVERS ON FOREIGN FISHING VESSELS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my colleagues have spoken several times before in this House, denouncing the Government's abuse of the NEED Program. Obviously their words were not heeded, because this abuse continues to spread. In a couple of weeks the over-the-side herring sale program will be getting under way in the Bay of Fundy. The Department of Fisheries and Oceans traditionally provides observers on the foreign vessels whose owners are here to buy fish from our fishermen. This year, however, those
observers are not being rehired. Instead these duties will be performed by workers on a NEED grant.
The lion's share of the work done by these observers is troubleshooting any problems which arise between our fishermen and the foreign vessel owners. This kind of work requires a 24-hour a day commitment for extended periods, in unfamiliar and sometimes hostile and unpleasant conditions. Can we really expect the recipients of NEED funds to put up with these kinds of conditions for only $200 per week? It is quite possible that many of them do not know they are getting into. A similar program tried a few months ago with Canadian offshore vessels fell apart after a couple of weeks because many of the participants resigned after they found out what the conditions were like.
The Government is using the NEED Program to replace higher paid skilled workers with lower paid untrained ones. It is becoming a restraint program, not a job-creation program. In this case our fishing industry could suffer seriously.

speakeroldname: Mr. Dave Dingwall (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: CELEBRATION OF CAPE BRETON'S MINING HISTORY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as the sitting Member for Cape Breton-East Richmond, an area proud of its coal mining tradition, we approach Miners' Memorial Day, on Saturday, June 11, 1983, with a sense of pride and a sense of sorrow. On this date we are reminded of the history of coal mining in Cape Breton and of the role coal mining has played in the shaping of our community. Mining on the Island dates back to 1720. Many technological advances have evolved since then. While mining methods have changed over the years, the unique qualities of the miner, which can be best described in one word, courageous, have not.
The struggle of the miner has not been without adversity. We remember the fight to bring in the United Mines Workers of America and the infamous strike of 1909-1910; the six years of protest culminating in the strike of 1925 and the tragic death of William Davis, killed 58 years ago; the Number 12 mine explosion of 1917, and more recently, the explosion in 1979. Over the years there have been triumphs and disasters. At this time we remember the contributions made by all miners and their families, and honour those who lost their lives.

ORDER TO DISMANTLE PEACE CAMP ON PARLIAMENT HILL
speechtext:

Madam Speaker, through its grant program the Medical Research Council provides support for research projects in health sciences whether basic, applied, or clinical.
Currently, at Princess Margaret Hospital in Toronto, and at a number of selected centres in Canada, bone marrow transplants are being carried out for leukemia patients. This is a well controlled, collaborative study designed to improve transplant techniques and to evaluate the benefit of transplants in comparison with conservative management. Preliminary results are most promising and encouraging, but it will be another two years before it can be said whether transplants will make a significant breakthrough in the search for a leukemia cure.

CONDEMMATION OF GOVERNMENT POLICIES AFFECTING FARMERS IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, there is a very real crisis in western Canadian agriculture today, due to a number of factors. A combination of rising costs, declining grain prices, disastrously high interest rates, and inadequate Government policies, have forced many farmers to the verge of bankruptcy.
Unfortunately, the Government's energy and transportation policies have added substantially to this problem. While many improvements are needed, two changes can be made immediately. First of all, the farmers' very substantial operating costs can be and should be reduced by abolishing the 9 per cent federal sales tax on farm fuels and fertilizers.

June 9, 1983

Second, the prairie farmer must be guaranteed that his transportation costs never exceed the long term average. subtopic: CONDEMMATION OF GOVERNMENT POLICIES AFFECTING FARMERS IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: SUPPORT FOR PROGRESSIVE CONSERVATIVE PARTY AMENDMENT
SUPPORT FOR PROGRESSIVE CONSERVATIVE PARTY AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) have stated in the House a number of times that they wanted consensus in the West on changes to the Crow rate policy. The freedom of choice amendment recommended by the Progressive Conservative Party and the Hon. Member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) in this House is an acceptable framework for agreement.
This amendment has received wide acclaim in western Canada, and at public meetings the vast majority of a crosssection of farmers, almost unanimously, supported the concept. This is understandable, as the freedom of choice option goes right back to basic democratic principles; the people who have to live with the program decide what the program will be. Real democracy! Producers themselves will decide whether their share of the Crow shortfall will go to the railways or to the producers. The producers choosing to take the shortfall themselves will then decide to use the railway or the trucks, or feed their grain to livestock. This freedom of choice will hurt no one but will be a unifying force in Canada. The program will provide the instrument which will permit all industries in the West to reach their real potential, and it will hurt no one in any part of Canada.
I urge the Government to accept this amendment. It will do much to unite Canada. The freedom of choice concept will guarantee the consensus which the Prime Minister and the Minister of Transport said they were seeking.

Madam Speaker, I would like to ask a question of the Minister of Transport relating to the problem of the West Coast grain handling dispute. As the Minister will know, grain exports account for billions of dollars and are very important not only to western Canada but to the whole economy as well. I understand that there has been no negotiation between either labour or management since June 1. I wonder if the Minister can give us an update regarding this very critical situation on the West Coast.

speakeroldname: Hon. Lloyd Axworthy (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I might reply on behalf of the Minister of Labour who is still overseas, but who, we all hope, will be back very soon. We have responded to their telegram, suggesting to them that any attempt to introduce mediation or conciliation must first be preceded by a clear example that they themselves are willing to come to the table and get down to bargaining so that an arrangement or decision can be made in that kind of spirit. There is no point in intervening someone in that particular situation until both parties clearly demonstrate their own willingness to arrive at an agreement.

Madam Speaker, I would point out to the same Minister that the Government has a responsibility in that, in 1974, through the Neil Perry Report it gave parity with longshoremen to the grain workers. As of last year, 1982, there has been a conflict because the Government imposed a six and five package on grain handling companies Therefore the Government has a responsibility in this situation because there is a conflict of Government policies which both parties are trying to work out. Would the Minister reconsider his position so that the Government would become involved, either by appointing a commission or a board to become directly involved, to ensure that some face to face negotiations take place again between labour and management?

speakeroldname: Hon. Lloyd Axworthy (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I think we in this House are all deeply concerned that an agreement be reached. No one, in any way, wants to witness the kind of blockage of transportation of our grain which has happened in the past. However, I must say that absolutely no good is being served by members of the Opposition standing up in the House trying to negotiate a settlement across the floor of the House of Commons. The negotiation must take place between the parties to the dispute. That is what collective bargaining is all about.
June 9, 1983

Madam Speaker,
I point out to the Minister that it is not a question of any good being done by the Opposition. The reason that we are asking the Minister to do something is because the Government is doing no good in this situation.
Question.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister. He knows that the Government decision on the Crow has resulted in a cap being put on the export of grain of about 31.1 million tonnes. This will cost the nation about $4 billion to $5 billion by 1990, whereas an investment of $150 million a year to remove that cap would result in the nation being richer by $4 billion or $5 billion. Madam Speaker, there is no cap on the export of grain from Canada, none whatsoever. The Bill presently before the House states, however, that there would be a cap on the contribution that the Government of Canada will make to grain transportation. There is a big difference between the two. That was a suggestion made by the Gilson group, and the Government of Canada had accepted that simply as an indication that there is a limitation on the amount of money the federal Government can put into the transportation of grain.
Should the farmers of Canada prefer not to have the cap, that is a suggestion I am quite willing to receive, but only inasmuch as it would be understood that this would not affect the total amount of the contribution of the federal Government.
In specific answer to the question, the fact is completely different from the implication. It is estimated that the amounts of grain exported by Canada will move from 31 million tonnes to 42 million tonnes by the end of the decade.
Madam Speaker, the farmers are paying 10 per cent of the price up to 31 million tonnes. If they pay 100 per cent beyond that, that is an effective cap.

Madam Speaker, the fact is that when Gilson produced his report he had a number of supporters; there is no doubt about that. As it is not possible to have everybody agreeing with every part of it, the poor Minister of Transport has been begging people kindly to settle for 65 per cent or 75 per cent of their interest and their points of view on the subject. Hopefully, he will get that soon.

subsubtopic: SEIZURE OF CHILDREN'S THEATRE COMPANY FUNDS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to direct a question to the Minister of National Revenue. A few months ago officials of Revenue Canada moved in and seized the funds of Carousel Players, a children's theatre company based in St. Catharines, Ontario, which has been entertaining children for many years. These funds were seized on the pretext that the theatre company had failed to make remittances for UIC and Canada Pension Plan contributions. The Minister must know that virtually all theatre groups in Canada operate on the basis that actors are considered selfemployed. They are very seldom employed. Will the Minister clarify his Department's position on this matter? With this action, is the federal policy being changed with respect to
Canadian artists? If this is the case, what other Government Departments or agencies have been consulted in this area?
[ Translation]

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre Bussieres (Minister of National Revenue):
subsubtopic: SEIZURE OF CHILDREN'S THEATRE COMPANY FUNDS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, for several years, the Department of National Revenue has been examining the insurability and nature of the employment of the persons in question. After a thorough study, it was determined, according to the customary criteria used by the Department, that their employment was insurable under the provisions of the Unemployment Insurance Act and the Canada Pension Plan Act. In the circumstances, the Department has no alternative but to request that both employee and employer pay their share of the unemployment insurance and Canada Pension Plan premiums. This was done, without prejudice to employees, employers or the work they are doing, and in accordance with the legislation now in effect.

Madam Speaker, can the Minister tell us whether it is the intention of the Department to move on other theatre groups across the country and do to them what was done to the Carousel group? Does the Minister realize that the arts community is very concerned about the effect this kind of policy will have on the work which these theatre groups do? I ask this because many of these people are employed sporadically and temporarily.

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre Bussieres (Minister of National Revenue):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, what the Hon. Member just said merely confirms that a thorough study of each specific case must be made before the Department can decide as to the insurability or non-insurability of employment. The Department looks at the employee's status vis-a-vis his employer and also considers whether or not his employment is permanent, and a final decision is made on the basis of these criteria. It does not mean that a decision made in this particular situation will necessarily apply to other cases. I am merely pointing out that a thorough study is made of the case before a final conclusion is reached.

On the first point made by the Hon. Member, the fact that the last allotted day this year would be in mid-June was well known by my colleague. I told him in advance that we are experimenting with parliamentary reform and that after June 15 we will have long sitting days. During this period of supply beginning after Easter, we have given the Opposition 12 allotted days so far. That is a lot of time that has been used by the Opposition. I think it is very reasonable that the last allotted day is to be before days with extended sitting hours. Even though we are acting under the new parliamentary reform, I would like to tell my colleague that in the past when hours were not extended it often happened that the last allotted day was somewhere around June 17, 18 or 19. June 9, 1983
Order Paper Questions CLOSED CAPTIONED PROGRAMS

1.	What is the policy of the Canadian Radio-Television and Telecommunications Commission concerning the desire of cable companies to decode closed-captioned American programs instead of being forced to substitute Canadian signals that are not closed-captioned for the hearing impaired?
2.	Have efforts been made by the CRTC to encourage broadcasters to (a) produce Canadian close-captioned programming (b) purchase closed-captioned versions of foreign programs and, if so, what were such efforts?

I am
informed by the Canadian Radio-Television and Telecommunications Commission as follows:
1.	The Canadian Radio-Television and Telecommunications Commission requires cable licensees that have 6,000 or more subscribers to substitute for local or regional signals when requested by the local or regional broadcaster under the provision of section 19 of the Cable Television Regulations.
Two cable licensees now have authority to decode closed-captioned programming. The Commission is currently reviewing an amendment that would allow these and other cable licensees to apply for specific exemptions to the requirement to perform program substitution when lower priority signals are captioned. The Commission hopes to announce its decision on these measures in the near future.
2.	This Commission has always taken the position that it is the broadcaster's responsibility to determine how they will spend their resources to serve its minority constituents. Broadcasters who are before the Commission for various reasons may be questioned on their programming efforts. Questions concerning service often arise and as part of that discussion, the subject of captioning may be raised. The subject may be raised by the Commission itself or it could be raised as part of an intervention from any interested member of the public.
The Chairman of the Commission has written each independent television broadcaster and cable company on services and programs for the disabled pointing out how important service to the hearing impaired is and, at the same time, soliciting their comments.
This subject has also been raised with some of the pay television licensees.

The first thing to do is acknowledge that the Government program is not at an acceptable level. This morning my colleague, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie), outlined the kind of intellectual bankruptcy and basic dishonesty of the approach of the Conservative Party. The
June 9, 1983

Hon. Member who just spoke did not outline what the Conservative Party would be prepared to do to face the problems of the industry. He stated no policy and no position, but just said that there are too many problems and that that is the fault of the Liberals.
I should like to ask the Hon. Member what the Conservative Party would do about corporate concentration in the newspaper and media sector. What would it be prepared to do about a small number of people controlling a large number of media outlets and controlling retail outlets that depend on those for media advertising, squeezing out other competitors and destroying a competitive system?

I challenge the previous speaker to put up some alternatives by which the Canadian people would judge his Party, or at least admit that his Party is prepared to see concentration continue to the detriment of consumers and to other small businesses in Canada. What is that Party prepared to do to ensure there is a diversity of titles?

Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to receive the challenge and to be able to respond to it. The first assertion made by the Hon. Member was to the effect that companies which had retail outlets were squeezing out retail competitors. I would ask the Hon. Member to supply justification for that statement. I think he will not be able to do so. Hon. Members would be interested if he could.
He asked about the issue of cross-media ownership. If he had followed the proceedings of the CRTC over the years, he would have known that the CRTC has always had the right and has always insisted upon the right, to question cross-media ownership. There is nothing new in these proposals that goes beyond what the CRTC was able to do before.
Finally, the Hon. Member asked what sort of positive proposals this Party has. I have made a number of proposals, including some for changes in the tax laws. An example is the case of the Blackburn holdings in London. The London Free Press is owned by a family operation. As the tax laws stand, if Mr. Blackburn were to die, his family might be forced to sell the newspaper to a chain or some other buyer and be forced to divest themselves of those holdings. This could lead to greater corporate concentration.
My criticism of the Government's proposals and of the NDP "me too" approach is that they are strictly interested in regulating a dwindling number of dailies. They have not proposed anything that would improve the climate in which newspapers would operate. For example, they do not propose changes to the tax legislation to encourage advertising, which is the lifeblood of Canada's daily newspaper industry. Second, the great issue that we should be concerned about is diversity in the media. We are concerned about the ability of Canadians
Supply
to draw their opinions from a number of different sources. The best way to ensure that is to ensure diversity.
The position taken by the NDP and the Liberal Government over the years, particularly as it relates to the electronic media, has been to draw an electronic curtain along the 49th parallel and say that we should restrict competition rather than encourage it. They cannot have it both ways, Mr. Speaker.
I say that competition should be encouraged both in the electronic media and in the print media. Canadians would be far better served by that than they would by a restrictive regime that regulates a dwindling number of dailies and ensures that friends of the Government are able to pass judgment on what working journalists have said and done.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I enter this debate today because of the things that people say, and some people may even believe what they say. The motion reads as follows:
That this House rejects the centralizing and interventionist policies of the Government as an ideological thrust aimed at introducing socialization of the Canadian economy by the back door and without the authorization of Parliament, and a definite and present threat to the freedom of Canadians.
Crown corporations have been a way of life in Canada for many years. To suggest at this time that they are socializing our country is plain nonsense, nothing more than nonsense. Let us look at Canada. Owing to the size of this country, with its very small population and diverse regions, Canada is faced with problems that smaller or more compact countries do not have to deal with. It became obvious early in Canada's history that some services that Canadians required could not be provided equitably by private enterprise. If we relied on profitmaking private business to meet all the needs of Canadians, there would be a lot of well-off people living in the Quebec-Windsor corridor and a few people scattered in pockets around the rest of the country.
With respect to the Crowsnest Pass freight rate, which Hon. Members opposite are so determined to keep us from changing, it was interesting to read in the press yesterday what the candidates for the leadership of that Party are saying about the Crowsnest Pass freight rate. I believe every one of them has said it has to be changed. I believe one of them is quoted as saying that it should be scrapped completely. I do not know what will happen to him in the leadership contest. The former Leader of that Party says he does not know enough about it to make a comment. At least, that is what he was reported in the press as saying. That sounds kind of strange to me.
That Party opposite is determined, Mr. Speaker, to keep us from changing the Crow rate. It must be changed because of our very recognition that it is not fair to ask farmers on the Prairies to carry the full cost of transporting their grain to export markets when the beneficiary of that trade is the entire population of Canada. Governments over the years have recognized their responsibility was to unite Canadians. One of the best ways to do that is to provide real opportunity for all. If

June 9, 1983
Supply
private industry could not, or would not, then it was the legitimate role of government to step in. Crown corporations were the vehicles which were used. I do not believe any one of those Crown corporations even intentionally abused that power.
If Crown corporations are socializing Canada, then it is a process which has had the full blessing of the Progressive Conservative Party. The first and some of the biggest Crown corporations formed in this country were instituted by Conservative Tory Governments. For example, the Canadian Wheat Board, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and the Canadian National Railways were all fathered by Conservative Governments. I do not believe any Hon. Members, Mr. Speaker, would seriously argue that these Crown corporations have not worked effectively for Canada. I do not hear any strong calls for their abolition or fears that they are turning Canada into a socialist country.
I can remember travelling with the previous head of Canadian Pacific Railways and the head of the CNR. We were visiting a proposed construction site between Calgary and Kamloops on the CP route and between Kamloops and Edmonton on the CN route. Some of the people on the trip said afterwards: "You know, the head of CP sounded more like he was running a Crown corporation than did the head of CN". They thought the heads of the two railroads, by their philosophy, should be interchanged because of the way they were putting forth suggestions as to what should be done in the railroad industry and what should be done for the good of Canada.
The Canadian Wheat Board, Mr. Speaker, is one of the most successful grain sales agencies in the whole world. Other countries send their officials here to study it. Farmers in other countries urge their governments to follow the Canadian pattern. You must remember the "great American grain robbery" of the 1970s when the Russians secretly bought so much United States grain that they upset the world market. That could not have happened if the United States had had a national sales agency which kept on top of what grain was sold to what country. That cost the United States farmers, Mr. Speaker, billions of dollars. What did the U.S. Secretary of Agriculture do in that so-called great free enterprise country? He moved in and put export controls on, because they were shorting the market. They were making a scarcity of grain in that country. However, the Russians "capitalized", if I can use that word, and made almost 100 per cent profit on all the grain which they bought. They moved into that system and bought it up and did it in such a refined, professional way that no one knew what they were doing until it was too late.
Crown corporations, Mr. Speaker, are not confined solely to the federal Government. Every Province has some. So they should, because every Province has the same basic problem as the Government of Canada has, that is, how to provide equal levels of service and opportunities to residents in regions with different natural resources.
I do not hear the Hon. Members opposite, Mr. Speaker, criticizing provincial Governments for socializing the country by setting up Crown corporations. In Saskatchewan there is a
huge Crown corporation which looks after potash in that Province. I said to the Deputy Premier, the House Leader and the Minister of Agriculture of that Province the other day: "Are you going to sell the Saskatchewan Potash Corporation?" The answer was: "Of course not; it is making money for us." I said: "Have you got rid of any of the Crown corporations which the previous Government had?" The answer was: "Not yet". I don't know if they are going to get rid of any of them either, because they have been a good thing for that Province.
They have in Saskatchewan, for instance, a transportation system which is owned by the Province and which provides large, smooth-riding, air-conditioned buses all over those roads which are built by the Province. Is that centralizing? Is that socializing? Roads at one time, Mr. Speaker, used to be toll roads. Now they are paid for by everyone. They are paid for by the few who say: "We do not use them; why should we pay for them?" I have not heard one suggestion from the other side that the highway system should go to a toll type of system, that anyone who uses highways in Canada, whether municipal, provincial or federal, should pay a toll charge on them. I have not heard that being suggested. I have not heard that the Members opposite would go back that far in their medieval thinking. However, they have suggested it in some other ways.
I wonder if they should think also of our educational system. Maybe they call that system centralization also. I remember when I first came to this House, the Government gave $26 million to the schools of higher learning in this country. Mr. Pearson was Prime Minister at that time. He said that every young Canadian should have equal opportunity to education. He was going to fund universities and schools of higher learning for those people he described at that time, those "who may live in have-not Provinces which do not have the resources to go ahead with that type of system". Last year this Government gave $4 billion to the schools of higher learning. Are the Members opposite suggesting that that is "centralizing", when education is strictly under the Provinces? They have the control, yet at the present time we are paying over 50 per cent of all administration costs for education. Are the Members opposite suggesting that that is what we should get rid of?
Are they suggesting our church system in Canada, where everyone contributes if they want to, and everyone can attend if they want to, is "socialization" or "centralization"? Are the Members opposite suggesting our parks system in this country is "socialization" or "centralization"? Is that what Members opposite are suggesting, that we should get rid of all those and let someone in the private sector run them? Are they suggesting that our natural harbours and our man-made harbours are something which should be turned over to the private sector? Are they suggesting that Air Canada be turned over to some private system because it is a Crown Corporation and is under a Liberal Government?
Is the mover of this motion suggesting, perhaps, Mr. Speaker, that because Pacific Western Airlines is in the Province of Alberta and owned by the Province of Alberta, that that is free
June 9, 1983

enterprise because it is under a Conservative Government? Is he suggesting something like that? Does it mean that Air Canada is "centralization" or "socialization" because it is owned by the federal Government and run by the federal Government for the people of Canada, but PWA, because it is in the Province of Alberta, is different?
Is the Hon. Member suggesting, for instance, when freedom of choice on the Crow rate was talked about earlier, something the same as Alberta has for the irrigation districts in Alberta? Under law in Alberta, if you do not turn over the ownership of the headworks of all the irrigation systems in Alberta, you do not share-and that is freedom of choice-in the S234 million special fund which is set aside to assist these people. Is that what Hon. Members opposite call "freedom of choice"? I have met these people. Is PFRA, for instance, "socialization" or "centralization"? These are people who are offering engineering services and so on, and they have made a tremendous contribution to western Canada. Are Hon. Members opposite suggesting that we abolish PFRA?
We set it up.
Yes, that is another one. The Hon. Member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) has asked me to find more funds for the Farm Credit Corporation.
Of course.

That is a Crown Corporation. Does he want me to centralize all farm lending in Canada under the Farm Credit Corporation? Is that what he is saying? Is that more "socialization"? Is that what he means? He should say what he means.
In the Province of Alberta the Treasury Board has banks all over the Province. Is the Hon. Member suggesting that perhaps we should get into the bank business? It is probably called private enterprise if it is in Alberta; however, if you suggest it for Canada, you are becoming a very bad socialist.
Over half of the land in Alberta is owned by the state. Most of the mineral resources in Alberta are owned by the state and administered by the State. I do not understand what the Members opposite mean when they talk about "socialization" and "centralization". I can remember when the Government was told to get rid of grain elevators. So I put them up for sale. I can see that the Hon. Member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil) remembers it very well. Who bought them in Alberta? That great private enterprise system called the Alberta Government. That was not centralization or socialization because it was under a Conservative Government in Alberta. Therefore they call it private enterprise in Alberta. But when I had them under the Canadian Grain Commission, that was Liberal socialization. I do not understand why when it is good for one, it is not good for the other.
Take the Opposition's view on the media, for instance. How is centralizing under a huge private corporation to have the media under one control any different? When the Government
Supply
suggests something to try to protect the little person in the media in some manner, the Opposition say that it is bad and that we are interfering. I do not understand how it can be said that the free enterprise system in the media system is working properly when more and more central control takes over in that fashion.
When we were talking about Canagrex in recent days, we heard a lot about how it would own farms. They made a comparison with Russia and Poland. No Russian farmer has the say that the Canadian farmer does. No Polish farmer has the say. It is wrong to make that kind of comparison because freedom of choice will be made and Canagrex cannot be involved in farm ownership. It cannot be involved in any of the things that they mentioned. It can only get involved when asked, and only in exporting.
One Hon. Member mentioned the other day that we would find cans on the shelves with Canagrex written on them. That cannot happen in Canada because Canagrex can only be involved in products for export. The Opposition called it socialism and the taking over of the last bit of free enterprise in Canada.
Those Members have heard me and know how well that I understand and appreciate agriculture in Canada. I recently met with Mr. Gorbachev here who was from the Politburo. I must say that he was entertained royally in Alberta. I appreciate their paying for part of the Bill. He met with the Premier of Alberta when he was there. The Premier of Alberta is paying $40 a tonne in subsidy on canola crushing plus $9 a tonne freight assistance. Who was he trying to sell it to? The Soviet Union. The Premier was saying what a great product it was, and I agree, but he is giving the Soviet Union $49 a tonne more than Saskatchewan or Manitoba could. He has the resource of a great pile of money which he can take out by the handful now and again. He could control the canola industry in Alberta if he continued this long enough because the other industries would be depleted both in Saskatchewan and in Manitoba.
I have direct responsibility for several Crown corporations and agencies. I assure all Hon. Members that they work well on behalf of the Canadian farmers and Canadian consumers. The Agricultural Stabilization Board and the Agricultural Products Board have used Canadian taxpayers' dollars wisely to keep the agri-food industry financially strong and viable. The Hon. Member for Essex-Kent (Mr. Daudlin), who spoke to me just before I rose, came to tell me how well the Agricultural Products Board was working with the food processing industry in Ontario in order to save it by buying its product. He was saying how it worked well with the Province of Ontario on loan assistance it had given to a canning factory and how the two Governments were accomplishing this. Does centralization or socialization mean making sure those industries stay alive? I do not think it is. I think that is what we want.
I heard one Hon. Member talking in the House recently about Koreans and using brainwashing tactics, that if you told people often enough, you wore them down and they believed it.

I have never heard any better description of what the Opposition were doing when saying what Canagrex would do to our society.
The Agricultural Products Board has had the power to buy and sell since 1952. I would ask Members to do some research and find any time when that Board has had its powers abused by any Minister, whether Liberal or Conservative, since that time. They will find that it has not been abused.
What can the Agricultural Products Board do? It can buy up surplus quantities of food production to forestal market disruption and then put it back into the system when prices are stable. We have bought grapes that have been turned into brandy. It was made from red grapes when people discontinued drinking red wine. I can tell those Members that if they want some brandy, they can even use for Sacramental wine if they wish; it is of high quality. Our rules and regulations for making brandy or any spirited beverages are much more strict than those of any other country in the world.
Let me return to the Farm Credit Corporation because that is one of my favourite topics. While Hon. Members on the other side may be as honest, I wish they would show the honesty shown by the Hon. Member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) when he talks about the Farm Credit Corporation. He has said that it must have more funding to look after the needs of farmers. I see his colleague, the Hon. Member for Moose Jaw nodding his head in full agreement. At one time the Farm Credit Corporation had 60 per cent of all long-term credit mortgage loans in Canada. We then asked the private sector to move in. The private sector moved in in a big way. We dropped down to 22 per cent of long-term mortgages for farmers in Canada. Then all hell broke loose. When the farmers called for long-term mortgages, what did the private lending institutions say? They told them to go to the Farm Credit Corporation. We have lists upon lists and applications upon applications.
Do not take over the farms. That is what we are saying.

When I have to go to the money market I hope to get the support from those Members to get that money for the Farm Credit Corporation. I hope they will not then say that the federal Government is again increasing its debt load and affecting its credibility in the rest of the world.
Let them be honest when they talk about socialization in the agricultural industry. With respect to my share of the federal budget, no country in the world spends as little per capita as we do on agriculture. No country in the world has as healthy an agriculture industry as we do. If those Members want to talk about socialism and communism, let them see how much money those countries pour into agriculture. They would be very pleased to have only half of the agriculture industry that we have. A member of the Russian Politburo who visited us was quite honest when we showed him our meat packing plants, our food processing plants, our dairy farms, beef farms, and grain farms. He was utterly amazed at what he saw. He
said, "I heard so much about it but I had to come and see for myself."
Certainly our industry was built by agencies such as the Farm Credit Corporation, the Agricultural Products Board and the Canadian Dairy Commission. It was built by these agencies, and some people call that centralization or socialization. But they are necessary in our country. When they talk about proliferation, let me say that I could have brought Canagrex in by Order in Council. I chose the legislative route. Some farmers have said I am wrong, but I think it has been an education for many people here.
I can go on to talk about all the great things we have done to build this country and its agriculture industry, which has been the envy of such huge countries in the northern hemisphere as China and the Soviet Union as well as many smaller countries in the northern hemisphere in regions that are similar to ours. We have long cold winters and a short growing season. I find what we have been able to do in our country phenomenal.
I see, Mr. Speaker, that you are making motions-

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Minister spoke about going to the money market for funds for the Farm Credit Corporation. The Corporation did, in fact, go to Europe and borrowed money at, I believe, 12.75 per cent. For a number of years Members on this side have promoted an agri-bond concept and another concept regarding capital gains tax whereby the Farm Credit Corporation could borrow money at about half that rate. The Minister has never made any attempt, as far as we can determine, to implement that concept. If he is interested in the farmers of this country and in having cheap money available to them, why has the Minister not been trying to sell that concept to Cabinet? Would he tell us that, please?

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member knows full well that the committee appointed to look into how the investments of banking systems should work recommended very strongly against that. They were people mostly from what we call the blue chip committee because they were from the lending institutions. There was consultation with the Government, and they did not recommend that concept. I still think it is a very good idea.
The Hon. Member if wrong when he talks about the money borrowed. We borrowed money at 11.25 per cent in Canadian funds for ten years repayable in ten years in Canadian funds. It is a very good rate of interest we were provided. None of the lending institutions at the present time will lend anything, as
June 9, 1983

far as I know, over three years at a fixed interest rate. The last rate I had quoted for three years was 15.75 per cent. The Hon. Member knows very well that we have entered into an agreement with the Province in which he lives, that is, Saskatchewan. It has a loan program to assist young farmers who are starting out. That program is one whereby we lend the money to them, the Province moves in and funds are subsidized by 5 per cent. It brings the interest rate down to 8 per cent for young farmers for the first five years of the mortgage. The Province of Ontario is trying to negotiate such a program at the present time for its young farmers. Neither one of those Provinces is promoting the agri-bond, and they are Conservative Provinces. If we got the support of those Provinces, probably we would have more support in getting the program through the Government of Canada. The Hon. Member for Moose Jaw could use his influence with the Conservative Government of Saskatchewan and perhaps get it to say "We want the agri-bond system". I believe, as the Hon. Member for Moose Jaw does, that it is a good system. But I have not been successful in getting it through.

Mr. Speaker, I am disappointed the Hon. Minister has been unable to get the scheme through Parliament. He talks about listening to a committee made up of high calibre lending people, and so on. If the Minister is seriously concerned about the plight of the farmers and there is a way to make this money available without subsidization, surely he must be able to sell Cabinet on it. If he is unable to sell the system to Cabinet on his own, perhaps he would like to invite some Members from this side of the House to go with him and make representations to Cabinet.
You will never get into Cabinet that way.

If the Minister is serious, not only will he be helping the farmer by lowering interest rates but he will also help those farmers who have spent a lifetime building up their farm assets cut back on their capital gains tax. Many farmers have spent their lifetime building up their farm assets. They have no ready cash. They look forward to the day when they can sell their farm and equipment and have the money to buy a house in the city. But by the time the Government takes its share of income tax and capital gains, there is nothing left with which the farmer can build a home.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member questions my sincerity about this. I have checked the records and I do not believe I saw his name or that his Party presented a brief to this committee on the very thing he is proposing today in the House. They had that opportunity They were invited to do that kind of thing. Anyone could make a presentation to the committee when the hearings were being held. I may have missed it by omission, but I am sure the Hon. Member, who speaks with such sincerity about this today, must have presented a brief.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister. In the motion we are discussing today it suggests that the
Supply
federal Government is centralizing policies and has interventionist policies. The Minister, in explaining the Government's decision, described the functions of the Dairy Commission and other marketing agencies. I understand there are a number of marketing agencies operating in the Province of Ontario. Could the Minister give me some information concerning these marketing agencies, which products are under the jurisdiction of these agencies and whether these agencies set up and operated by Conservative provincial Governments are different in any way from the agencies set up by the federal Government?

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member asks a good question. A lot of people are under the impression that all the marketing boards in Canada come under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Agriculture. Really there are only three marketing boards as such: the Egg Marketing Board, the Canadian Chicken Marketing Board and the Turkey Marketing Board. Then we have commissions. We have the Canadian Dairy Commission and we have the Canadian Wheat Board. Those are the main ones we have dealing with products in Canada. Each Province has many marketing boards. They are very powerful. They have control over supply and control in some instances, over price. They have an array of powers.
The Hon. Member says there is not one provincial Minister who would not want marketing boards, and actually I have never heard one provincial Premier of any Party, Conservative or other-but they are practically all Conservatives in Canada at the present time-say he does not want any more. Just recently we had a meeting of the signatories to the poultry agreements that we have for national marketing in Canada. What the Minister from Ontario said is recorded. He said that he was a strong believer in supply and management as long as these marketing boards are run well. I believe in Ontario there are forty-some marketing boards that have to do with products. Actually, Ontario and British Columbia were the creators of marketing boards. I believe it was British Columbia first. It goes back to 1928, I believe, for the dairy producers in the Fraser Valley, who had the first farming board to market milk.
One of the largest marketing boards, as we know, is the Canadian Wheat Board. People were not allowed a choice when the Wheat Board was imposed upon them by a Conservative Government. It was said that in Five years farmers would have a vote. The World War came along. They had an excuse for not having a vote. Farmers did not have a vote, I believe, until 1947 but then they voted about 85 per cent in favour of the Canadian Wheat Board. The Canadian Wheat Board is the largest marketing board in Canada. It has tremendous powers. It is protected against imports. You cannot import any grain under the authority of the Canadian Wheat Board unless you get a permit. That includes the Minister of Agriculture, Mr. Speaker. Even if he wants to bring in a bushel of grain for research, he has to get a permit from the Canadian Wheat Board to use that wheat in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to pose a question to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan). It pertains to the great job of intervention and protection of the public involvement, and it involves grain inspection in Canada. It pertains directly to agriculture and Government involvement.
It is my understanding that the Government intends to reduce the presence of meat inspectors in a variety of slaughterhouses and meat packing operations across the country and allow certain companies to undertake their own inspections under the authority of these meat inspectors even though they were not present. The responsibility for those seals would be placed in the hands of company officials. Basically, what would happen would be that the responsibility for supervision of the protection of the public and the degree of sanitation and health protection would fall on those who are to be regulated. Basically, the individuals who are to be regulated would be regulating themselves without adequate supervision and there would ultimately be a serious situation concerning public health. As I understand, there has already been a large number of violations and concerns about procedure in meat plants. In spite of this, the Minister and the Department intend to go ahead and reduce the presence of federal inspectors in those positions. Would the Minister be prepared to outline just how he can justify that kind of situation?

Madam Speaker, we will not downgrade the meat inspection in Canada. We will not cut our staff. If we had more funds, we would probably add more staff at the present time. In Canada, we have one of the best inspection services for meat products that there is in the world. One can make a comparison. We have 541 plants in Canada which are federally inspected, which are approved for export to the United States of America. In essence, what that means is that any meat we feel is good for domestic consumption is good for export, or vice versa. Some countries just have inspection for export to meet the standard. For instance, the United States, which is a big country, only has 141 plants which will meet our inspection criteria to export meat to Canada.
I know full well what the Hon. Member is discussing, because it involves a little plan in his area where consideration is being given to withdrawing an inspector who has been there, I believe, since the 1950s. That inspector has not been withdrawn, and I do not think that he will be, because the order that I issued was that he had to stay there, and that if a service had been provided for any length of time, there was no way we could downgrade it. In no way will we be allowing a company to do its own meat inspection and then try to export the product, because with the present international trade agreements, the product would not even be accepted.
As the Hon. Member knows, there is some inspection which is run by the Provinces. At one time there were many problems, and there has been a lot of publicity, but no significant breakdown in our inspection system has ever taken place. As far as I remember, when bad meat was being sold, and this type of thing, it was all out of provincially-inspected slaughtering and meat packing plants. There was a wild rush at that
time for us to provide inspectors for their meat plants with the CDA inspection stamp of approval on them. We did not have that many inspectors to do that. People recognized that it meant a pure, good product if it had the inspection stamp of approval from the CDA. If products are to be shipped across interprovincial or international borders, they must have that inspection. Some of the Provinces depend solely on the Canadian Department of Agriculture Inspection Service for their meat packing plants. Some of them have a combination of both federal and provincial inspection, and some are only provincially inspected plants, but in these cases, as far as I know, they are doing every bit as good a job as we are with the training that they are giving their people, the technicians and veterinarians on the job. There may be the odd time when we find people a little bit lacking, but if their lacks are pointed out to us, they are either fired or removed from their jobs, and that is for sure.

Madam Speaker, I listened carefully to the remarks of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan). I guess what really amazed me more than anything else, and I was trying to figure it out, is by what convoluted type of reasoning, when he was speaking of churches, highways and our education system, he was relating them to interventionism. I couid not quite understand it. What do churches and highways have to do with interventionism? I have listened to the Minister of Agriculture for four years. I guess we must give him credit for one thing: he is a master of bafflegab. However, I have never in my life heard anything like I heard today when he tried to relate churches, highways and our education system to interventionism. That really escaped me.
I just wonder how long the Minister believes he will fool the Canadian people with that kind of reasoning and nonsense, because that is what it is, just nonsense. I do not know whether the Minister knows it or not. Maybe he has been around here for so long that he does not understand it any more. All this nonsense just comes off him like water off a duck. I do not think that the Canadian people will put up with that kind of nonsense for much longer, not any longer than it takes us to get to the next election.
Do you think?

Canadian people have had it up to here with that kind of baloney, just baloney. If the Minister does not know this, I will not tell him, but Canadian people do not trust him. They do not trust his Government any more. Perhaps it is not so much because of interventionism. Does the Minister know why they do not trust the Government? They do not trust it because of what it let the former Minister do and how it rewarded its own at the public's expense. They do not trust it because the former Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources put one Michael Phelps on his payroll at public expense. He abused the public trust. That is why the Canadian public does not trust the Government. They do not trust it because the Minister of State for International Trade (Mr. Regan) uses
June 9, 1983

public transportation for the benefit of his own family. That is why the Canadian public does not believe in the Government any more. They do not trust it and they will kick it out.
We'll see about that.

I listened this morning to the laughter. Maybe it will not be too long before Eugene has the happy experience of joining the ranks of the unemployed in this country. Maybe if he were among those people he would understand the importance of a $1.4 billion loss which was incurred on the public's behalf. I wonder how all of the 1.5 million unemployed Canadians feel about that kind of waste, extravagance and gross mismanagement. I would be interested in knowing just how they feel about that. What they do not know, because the Government will not tell them, is about all the other disasters which are buried every day by the Government. Canadair is only the tip of the iceberg.
I listened with interest this morning to the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts). The Minister was to tell us all the good things his Government has done for Canadians. What the Minister really fails to understand is that what the Liberal Government has done over the last 15 years has been to destroy individual initiative in this country. The Minister does not have any appreciation whatsoever of that fact. It always seemed to me that the greatness of Canada was the greatness of our opportunity to go out and build, to create, to strive for something better in this life. In the last 15 years the Liberal Government has taken much of individual initiative away from Canadian people. That is why we are in this predicament today. Hon. Members on the other side of the House and those in the socialist Party to my left do not understand that that is at the core of the problem in the country today. What is individual initiative all about? That is what creates jobs. Governments do not create jobs. Governments spend money. Governments take in money with one hand and spend it with the other, and in the process about 30 per cent is lost.
I would like to refer to one thing which makes me so angry with the Government. When I return to my home riding of Calgary, I am saddened to see the needless devastation caused by the Government and its National Energy Program. Either it does not understand or it does not care. The Government has no idea what its National Energy Program has done to western Canada. Does it realize that there are 80 rigs running today in western Canada or how many there were before the National Energy Program was invented as a socialistic experiment of interventionism on a scale which had never been seen in the country before? Government Members ought not to be very proud of themselves. Are they proud of the 25,000 men they put out of work in the oil well drilling and servicing industry? Do they care? No, there is not a vote in western Canada. I can assure them that there will never be a vote for the Liberal Party in western Canada as long as I live. Let us remember the devastation that program has caused in western Canada. What for? Also it caused human misery. In aid of what? What has the National Energy Program accomplished? It is built upon bureaucracy. The people of Canada should know that the

They have Canadianized the oil industry, but they have bankrupted Canadian companies and foreign controlled companies are prospering as they never prospered before. The Canadian part of the industry is broke and bankrupt. This is why there are 80 rigs running in Canada. The National Energy Program is so good and so magnificent that there are 80 rigs in western Canada today looking for oil and gas!
That is because the price is down, and you know it.

The Hon. Member does not have the faintest idea what it is all about. He does not understand the industry and he does not care.
The saddest part of it is that I happen to know that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has stated that the National Energy Program is a disaster. The former Minister of Energy admitted in private that it is a disaster. The new Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Chretien) admitted that it is a disaster. Do they do anything about it? No, because that would be to admit that they made a mistake. The Liberal Government does not make mistakes; it has never made a mistake! Has anyone ever heard the Liberal Government over the last 15 years admit that it made a mistake? Is Canadair not its responsibility? That $1.4 billion lost by Canadair, is it not the Government's mistake? No, it indicates that it is the fault of the management of Canadair.
If I happen to be the president of a company or on the board of directors of a company, do I not have responsibility for the operations of the company? If it loses money, do I not have a responsibility to the shareholders? The Government and the Prime Minister are telling us that they are above all that, that it does not make mistakes and that it is management which makes mistakes. They tell us that it is not their problem because they appointed a bunch of Liberal hacks to the board of directors. Also they indicate that it is not their fault that it took six years to take off the financial statements of Canadair so that Hon. Members of Parliament would know where the company was going. They think that it is not their problem. The Minister of Agriculture would not understand the fiduciary responsibility which goes with his appointment as a Member of Cabinet. It is not their responsibility, they do not make mistakes, they are above making mistakes! I suppose they are not ordinary people and are not like the rest of us. They hold themselves above the rest of us. We are just ordinary people.
Over the last 15 years-and this is why I became a Member of Parliament-the Liberal Government has deliberately and

Canadians today are wondering why we are not as productive as some other countries in the free world. Canadians ask me why there are 1.5 million unemployed. Do you believe that?

I would not be here if I did not believe that. What do you think the Canadian Development Investment Corporation is doing? You believe that by forming this corporation with Mr. Joe Bell, the magnificent Senator Austin and Maurice Strong, it will save this country and Canadair, making it a viable operation together with de Havilland? Do you believe that this will contribute to the welfare of Canadians? Do you believe that Senator Austin, Joe Bell and Maurice Strong will do us any good? What have they accomplished in their whole lives, any one of the three of them? Zero. A great big zero. They got a law degree and that is the total sum of their contribution. The Liberals would probably do that because they know everything about everything. The Liberals believe, as do their partners in the NDP, that the guiding principle should be that more Government is better Government, big is beautiful, that we should have more Government, more regulation and ways to further control and redirect the lives of Canadians, telling them what they should be doing. We will see a lot more of that. It is not only the National Energy Program, but look at what the Foreign Investment Review Agency has done for us.
Most countries of the world, even the communist countries, are looking for investment capital. Most countries of the world want investment capital in order to provide jobs for their citizens and to build new industries. Not in Canada, no Sir! We want to slam the door on foreign capital.
Foreign-controlled companies that come to Canada should be good corporate citizens. However, that does not have anything to do with the money they put into this country. A dollar is a dollar in so far as creating a job is concerned. We should be creating a situation where we ensure that foreign capital behaves as a good corporate citizen, and that is all.
We need investment. This is a huge country desperately in need of capital today. There is a shortage of capital all over the world. To listen to the economic nationalists opposite, one would think we did not need any capital to create jobs for the 1.5 million unemployed Canadians.
The Government likes to intervene. It wants to control the media. It thinks there is a conspiracy among the media to tell the wrong things. It has the CBC to say what is right. We need $800 million Canadian taxpayer's money every year so that the CBC can tell us what the Liberal Government wants us to hear.
So far the Canadian newspaper industry has been privately owned. In the 50-odd years of my life, I thought the newpapers had done a reasonably fair job of recording the facts. What would concern me more about a corporate concentration in the newspaper industry would be for this Government to get its hands on it. Can you imagine the fun it would have controlling the media? Do you have any idea?
Every day each Cabinet Minister puts out a press release through his or her press secretary. Do you know how the press secretary earns his livelihood? It is by feeding the press information and news releases every day. It is a bigger propaganda machine than Herr Goebbels ever had.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct a question to the Hon. Member. In a recent issue of Business Week, an article on the Exxon Corporation stated that $4 million to $5 million was invested in an oil shale plant in Colorado and that the operation closed down before going into production because the price of oil had gone down. An article in a recent issue of Time magazine indicated that a large number of oil rigs were mothballed in the Gulf of Mexico, not working and not drilling. The United States has the most pro-business Government, a Government which believes in free enterprise, less control of business and less regulation, which it has had in 50 years, namely, the Reagan administration. That country does not have a Liberal Government or a National Energy Program, yet the energy industry in the United States is a way down from what it was a couple of years ago.
Is not the reason for that situation in the United States the reason for the similar situation in Canada, namely that two or three years ago the price of oil was expected to increase by 10 per cent or 15 per cent a year and that the price in a few years would be $70 or $80 a barrel? Is that not in fact the main reason why oil exploration and drilling has either stopped or been reduced dramatically, not just in Canada but in other countries as well, rather than the federal Government and the National Energy Program being entirely to blame?

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member makes a good point. It is interesting that he likes to apologize for the National Energy Program on behalf of the Government. I guess the socialists really helped in a lot of ways to create the National Energy Program. It is true that there has been a fall-off in exploration activity in the United States. There are really two parts to the explanation. First, the industry was very badly overbuilt in the United States. In the period around 1977, the industry in the United States was operating almost at capacity, with 2,000 land-based drilling rigs and about 60 offshore rigs in service. That inventory of drilling equipment was very rapidly expanded as the price kept going up, to a level of something over 5,000 landbased drilling rigs in the United States. So you can see, Mr. Speaker, that it increased by 150 per cent in a period of four years. The drilling industry in the United States has returned to about the same level of exploration as was being carried out in 1977 and 1978, and there is a very, very high level of exploration activity still proceeding in the United States with about 2,200 rigs at work.
I would also inform the Hon. Member that I happen to know that the industry is extremely active in the Gulf of Mexico at present. The United States has only a seven year supply of natural gas reserves left and the reserves of gas in the Gulf of Mexico are very sizeable and are being explored very aggressively.
Perhaps the Hon. Member could refresh my memory as to his question if I did not answer the latter part of it completely.

Mr. Speaker, my question was a very simple one. I asked the Hon. Member whether the drilling for conventional oil or the planning and building for the extraction of oil from shale rock in the United States or the extraction of oil from tar sands in Canada was predicated, by the industry and by the federal and Alberta Government, on the notion that the price of oil would go up 10 per cent or 15 per cent each year so that by the time the tar sands plants came onstream, the price of oil would be about $70 a barrel and would be competitive with conventional oil. That is not happening, and so I would ask the Hon. Member whether it would not be honest for him to admit that unless the price of oil will go up very substantially in the next few years, it will probably not be economically feasible for anybody, the Government of Canada, the Government of Alberta or private industry, to go ahead with tar sands or with very expensive conventional oil exploration.

First of all, Mr. Speaker, there is a very great difference between oil sands and oil shales. Extracting oil from oil shales in the United States is twice as expensive as extracting oil from oil sands in the Athabasca area of Alberta. Not only was Exxon but a good many other companies were optimistic about making a technological breakthrough that would allow them to recover oil from oil shales at something like $50 a barrel. In fact, those companies could not make that technological breakthrough that would reduce the cost to that level, and the cost would have been something in the order of $75 a barrel.
In the case of the oil sands in Canada, I think that it is fair to say that there would have been an advanced oil sands plant today had it not been for the punitive taxation that was introduced by the National Energy Program.

Mr. Speaker, many people in the country and in the House are faced with an interesting conundrum stemming from the immoral and dishonest approach of the Government. I could point to examples of this within the National Energy Program that really stand out. But on the other side of the coin, Mr. Speaker, is the basic dishonesty in the approach of the Conservative party to important questions dealing with the national energy policy.
I would point out that the Conservatives have failed to put one alternative on the record that would be acceptable or reasonable. The Conservatives criticize the Government without taking the responsibility of placing options before the people of the country. The Conservative Party would remove regulations and give control back to the multinational corporations. I would like to hear the Hon. Member from the Conservative Party talk about going to world oil prices and turning control back to the seven sisters in the country, which would basically put Canadian people out to hang.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member says that the Conservative Party does not make any positive recommendations about what it would do. A great many of my colleagues and myself have consistently said that first we would decontrol the price of domestic oil and natural gas and let it move to a market system. Second, we have said that we would scrap the
