Mr. Speaker, I enjoyed listening to the speech made by the Hon. Member for Calgary South (Mr. Thomson). He speaks passionately about what he believes in and that is what Parliament is all about. I always appreciate listening to him because he brings to Parliament a knowledge of his region and the industry with which he was involved. That knowledge is of great benefit to the debate. I always enjoy hearing politicians who have had a background in business speak because I am from a family that has always been in business. I studied business administration at university and I was briefly in business full time before I entered politics. I do enjoy hearing people with initiative who have been successful.
Where I depart from the Hon. Member's views, is where he suggests policies, because he displays his Party's impatience and sometimes almost intolerance for the other point of view. He speaks as though only the business point of view counted in matters of national interest. In his Party's view, when it comes time to implement public policy on behalf of the people, unless we follow to the letter whatever the industry wants to do or whatever business wants to do, either we do not know anything about it or we are supposed to listen to the view of business.
I suspect that my hon. friend will be in the House for a few years and I hope that with the years he will temper the opinion that he expresses so eloquently on that point of view with a little more realism and a little more appreciation for complex problems. Canada is a very complex country to govern. Particularly in the last two or three years, I feel that the approach of the Conservative Party to these very important national problems-the question of the National Energy Program, the question of the Constitution and a few other questions that have been of crucial importance to the country and have been debated in the House in the last few years-has demonstrated its incapacity to grasp the complexity of the problem. It continuously comes forward with simple solutions. Mr. Speaker, simple solutions to complex problems just do not work.
Somehow I think that the Conservative Party really does appreciate this. When I look at the motion of the Hon. Member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski), I see that it is very skillfully drafted. In that motion, there is a dimension in terms of Canadian politics that goes beyond the issue of intervention in the economy and beyond ideology and the question of more or less Government ownership or, as his motion reads, socialization. It also goes beyond the question of centralization in one level of Government or another. I do not understand why they
do not come out and say what they are expressing, only in part, and that is, some regional frustration. Some people in the Conservative Party who are spokesmen for their regional interest-and I do not fault them for that as it is their role to express that frustration-say through the Governmnent, "What you are doing to my region is wrong."
I do not understand why they want to mix the National Energy Program and the Constitution. I do not understand why it is not possible for them to say, in terms of industry and public policy, that we should have either more or less Government intervention in the energy sector. That is debatable, Mr. Speaker. What is the proper balance in a country like Canada on the question of how much Government intervention there should be? That is one issue.
Another issue is the regions versus the centre, one region versus another region or the centre versus one region. On the National Energy Program the Conservatives expressed a fear of socialization. But if they want to be honest, particularly those from Alberta, how can they be against Government intervention when their provincial Government, with which they do not dissociate themselves, is the most interventionist Government on energy matters in Canada? I do not want to make a judgment on that as it does not concern me that much, but the Alberta Conservative Government understands that on some of the issues it has Alberta's interests at heart and it does not deal with these problems simplistically.
When the Government of Alberta decides to buy an airline, I see that as a policy instrument, as a politicization of the economy in terms of saying it wants to have a transportation policy that will ensure the development of the economy of Alberta in the future. I do not see how Hon. Members opposite can be against having state intervention.
Hon. Members opposite talk about the disaster of the National Energy Program and the negative effects of the PGRT. They say it skims cash from the cash flow of companies. They do not say anything about the Alberta royalties that are the highest in the land, the highest of most western industrialized countries, royalties which skim the cash flow off the companies. If the Conservatives want to be honest with themselves they will realize that they have a responsibility to tell us where they stand on that issue. I can understand Members from Alberta and from the West generally expressing a regional frustration with the National Energy Program.
As a Liberal from eastern Canada I am very concerned. Even if I am not from the West and even if I do not have a background in the energy industry, I can understand that. The Hon. Member for Calgary South (Mr. Thomson) and a few other Members interjected a little while ago and demonstrated the intolerance they sometimes have for the other point of view. Apparently you are not supposed to know anything about the energy industry if you are from the East or if you are a Liberal or if you are not from the energy industry.

It is just that you prove it sometimes.

The Hon. Member for Lethbridge-Foothills (Mr. Thacker) says it is because I prove it sometimes. Hon. Members opposite prove a lot of things sometimes too. I have never said to a Member from another region of the country that he should not have a point of view on the fishery in the Atlantic Provinces or on the forestry policy because it is an industry that is important in my constituency. I do not tell them that they should not have anything to do with the 200-mile limit or the law of the sea because they are from a landlocked Province. I do not expect that they will have spent as much time on the dossier as I have, but I do not say that they should not be able to contest what I say. The day we start saying that, we have no tolerance for the other point of view.
Conservatives must become more responsible regarding these matters. As a Liberal from eastern Canada who has been here for the 15 years that are supposed to have been so terrible for the country, I admit that there is a regional dimension to the National Energy Program. Part of the concern in this Party, leading up to the years 1979-80, was for the national interest as we perceived it. I wish that in this country and in this Parliament particularly, one could speak one's mind about the national interest without being accused of being against another region. That burns me up, Mr. Speaker. Just because I give my perspective as a New Brunswicker-and that is not a powerful Province, economically or politically-then am I not supposed to give my view of the national interest because it may turn out to be a different view from that of Members from the West? That does not lead to mature debate. We should be able to have tolerance for those who disagree with us even if we express regional frustration, or it will become impossible to govern this country. It is a very complex country to govern in any event. In a certain sense we are governing the country against every natural and geographic factor. The Conservatives should understand that.
Why are the Conservatives having a leadership convention this weekend if this country is not a complex one to govern? Their own orientation as a Party is complex. They have their own problems in trying to determine where they should go. They know very well they are not involved in a leadership convention only because of the seasonal values of the Right Hon. Member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark), but because this country is confronted with very tough problems and choices. They have not been able to come out with a cohesive position on some matters. It is not a sin to admit that in your Party there is difficulty in coming to an orientation. If the country is simply to govern, why did the Conservative Party have a leadership problem? It is because some factions in that Party attempted to simplify the solution to those complex problems.
I have said that I admit there is a regional dimension to the National Energy Program. Should we have policy instruments that encourage more private sector involvement or instruments that encourage more federal or provincial Government involvement? Apart from that, there is the question of how a federal Government policy instrument affects the West. I can understand that westerners are going to be concerned about that. It is a legitimate question. If that is what they want to express,

they should express it clearly. They cannot try to bluff their way into this issue. They play with words and say that the centralizing and interventionist policies of the Government are an ideological thrust aimed at introducing socialization of the Canadian economy by the back door. It will be interesting to see if the new Tory Government in Saskatchewan is going to do away with all those Crown corporations. I do not believe it will, Mr. Speaker. It will make a judgment on what is best for the electors and the people of Saskatchewan.
Mr. Speaker, in my opinion, when we are dealing in the House with issues that have a regional dimension and concern the interests of one particular region in relation to the central authority, it is very important to discuss such questions in an atmosphere that encourages, mature and adult debate, in the course of which any comments that are made reflect tolerance for and patience with the views of those who come from other parts of the country.
In my speech, I would like to refer briefly to a speech made this morning, before the lunch recess, by the Member for Wellington-Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Beatty), when he said that in the last 15 years, or rather, to quote exactly what he said, when the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) retires, we shall find that in Canada, the rights of Canadians .. . and in my question, I asked him whether I had understood correctly, and he said yes, that the rights of Canadians had become more restricted compared to what they were in 1968. I then asked him how he could say that, when this was the party that had introduced language rights, first in federal Government institutions, and then as one of the mainstays of our plan to patriate the Constitution. Anyone who rises in the House and says the rights of Canadians have been circumscribed in the past 15 years is showing his ignorance of the fact that language rights are a social, human and public right. Technically, I would not say these are fundamental rights, but I do say that it is essential that the country should have language rights of this nature.
This Government, led by the Right Hon. Prime Minister, is the one that introduced the concept of enshrining rights and freedoms and language rights in the Canadian Constitution. This proposal was opposed in the House by the Progressive

Mr. Speaker, while the Hon. Member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) says in his motion that the policies of the Government are a definite and present threat to the freedom of Canadians, and the Member for Wellington-Dufferin-Simcoe is trying to say that the rights of Canadians are being circumscribed by the Government, I take great pride in saying that they are wrong and will continue to be wrong, that this is utter nonsense, and that Canadian political history will show that the period from 1965, even before the present Prime Minister came to power, until now, will be known as a period when the development of social, human, civil, political and fundamental rights, and that includes language rights, was unique in this country's history, and I would even go so far as to say that no other democracy in history can compare with the political development of Canada in this particular area.

Mr. Speaker, to say that the rights of Canadians were circumscribed during the last 15 years is superficial in the extreme or grossly partisan.
In fact, I strontly suspect, Mr. Speaker, that this morning, the intentions of the Member for Wellington-Dufferin-Simcoe were partly partisan. If he wants the floor, it is to speak to the rights of Canadians. I have the floor now, but I do not want to take up too much of the time of the House today. I could talk about how the Progressive Conservative Government in New Brunswick shows its concern for the rights of Canadians, the rights of the New Brunswick electorate. I will not do that now, Mr. Speaker, but if Progressive Conservative Members are anxious to talk about patronage, about circumscribing the rights of individuals, I could give a few examples of the concern of a Progressive Conservative Government for the rights of Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I always enjoy listening to the Hon. Member for Gloucester (Mr. Breau) and I appreciate the enthusiasm with which he engages in debate. He has implored all Hon. Members to exercise tolerance and understanding in the admission of mistakes. I would point out to him that, in the spirit of the environment within which the Hon. Member has made his pitch, perhaps he might want to consider the fact that the National Energy Program has been condemned by the industry. It has been condemned by Hon. Members in this House. It has been condemned by the workers
who have lost their jobs. Just recently, it has been condemned by the C.D. Howe Institute, which very categorically stated that the costs clearly outweigh the benefits of the National Energy Program and that there are less costly and disruptive means which could be expected to achieve the same or even superior benefits to the economy. What is really being said, Mr. Speaker, is that the goals and objectives of the National Energy Program, the three basic goals of fairness, equitable distribution and pricing, and self-sufficiency, have not been achieved.
Would the Hon. Member not consider now, even at this late date, to urge his Cabinet colleagues to take a second look and reassess the situation before the industry is destroyed completely? The Financial Post today headlines, "Oil rigs and services are barely hanging in". I am not sure whether the Hon. Member understands this, but most of our young western Canadians, or many of them, work in that kind of service and supply industry. They are now either out of a job or working south of the border. It is very serious.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member raises a very important question, and it is one which concerns me. I realize that the National Energy Program, being a fundamental change in the way policy was being designed in the energy area, is very controversial. I realize that. When you do something which is controversial, you are going to provoke a lot of reaction and a lot of opposition. It is true that a lot of people in the industry have criticized it. A lot of spokesmen from western Canada who are related to the energy interests have opposed it. But the Hon. Member cannot ignore the fact that with or without a National Energy Program, there was not going to be less searching for new oil and gas in Alberta and Saskatchewan in any event. We are at the stage of searching for secondary and tertiary recovery, as it is called in the industry. Whatever happened, there was to be shift away from the traditional search, which has gone on since 1945 for oil and gas in Alberta, to the so-called Canada lands. Therefore, the Hon. Member cannot ignore the fact that change was to come in any event. The Hon. Member cannot ignore, either, the fact that prices have gone down. He cannot ignore the fact that drilling has been reduced in the United States. It has been reduced all over the world. Therefore, to suggest that all of that is because of the National Energy Program is not to be totally fair.
I would ask the Hon. Member also to recognize once in a while that when the federal Government does something to help, as it did, for example, the gas industry in Alberta which has so many oil wells which are capped, and he knows why they are capped-they are capped because there are fewer markets-takes quite a risk. It took a risk when it approved the southern portion of the Alaska pipeline. He does not recognize the fact. He does not say that that was a risk we took

in terms of the interest of the country as those other than themselves perceive it, as well as in Alberta's interest. He does not say that in the latest change brought about by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Chretien) to permit the export of gas, in any event, to the United States, we have permitted the price to be reduced. Therefore, 1 wish the Hon. Member would balance his claims a bit with some recognition for the things the Government has done in the energy sector.

I have just one comment. I only want to point out that the shift of exploration activity from conventional areas to the offshore and frontier areas was not taken by the industry on its own. It was merely a shift as a result of a deliberate Government policy. For the information of the Hon. Member, the fact of the matter is that there are still ample conventional supplies which can be sought out. However, the fact concerning oil and gas is that the shift and emphasis has been placed on offshore, on the frontier areas, the result of which has been to see our conventional reserves depleting at the rate of 4 per cent per year.

Mr. Speaker, I do not totally disagree with the Hon. Member that the National Energy Program has had an effect on that. What I am saying to him is that there was a shift, in any event, as a result of economic forces, to the offshore and so-called Canada lands. However, he cannot ignore the fact that the Province of Nova Scotia and the Province of Newfoundland, for example, used all the political muscle they had. It is not a question of its being in the interest of the provincial Government only. They would want to persuade the federal Government to implement a policy regime as we did for the West in the late forties and fifties to permit the exploration of oil and gas of the shores of Nova Scotia and Newfoundland. Therefore, this shift came naturally, not only because of economic forces, which is part of the trend, and not only because of the actions of the federal Government, but also as a result of the natural expression of the political wish of Nova Scotia and Newfoundland that some of their money be invested off the shores of eastern Canada. The Hon. Member must admit that the shift of investment there is not totally owing to the National Energy Program or the federal Government.

Mr. Speaker, the other point that my friend, the Hon. Member for Gloucester, does not realize is that during the 1920s, when the level of technology swept across the western plains, only very shallow gas and oil deposits could be found, where it was obvious, because there were no machines to dig it up. Then, during the forties there was another wave, and during the seventies there was still another wave. Therefore, each time more advanced technology is utilized in the western plains enormous quantities of oil and gas are found.
The Pembina oil field, which is a tight field, was found because of that technology. The Hon. Member is indicating
Supply
that perhaps he does not appreciate that fact. There is much oil and gas there. Only as a comment I would like to say that it surely was not necessary, in order for the federal Government to become involved in the Canada lands and offshore, to bring in the National Energy Program which was so highly damaging to the West. It has virtually destroyed it. Why could the Government not have come up with a policy to develop these other areas without killing the conventional plains?

Mr. Speaker, I wish I had more time to answer these questions because, again, the Hon. Member forgets some facts, particularly while it is true that there is still some gas which could be found. The geological data is that there is much gas under the shales of Alberta, which has already been found and capped, and there is probably some more. However, the policy instruments which the Parliament of Canada implemented in the late forties, the fifties and the sixties, partly by the Diefenbaker Government and partly by the Liberal Governments, have provided the West with a policy and the taxation instruments which have permitted exploration there. How can he deny that other regions of the country which also have a potential for development of oil and gas should not be provided with policy instruments, too?
He didn't say that at all.

This is what the National Energy Program is doing. He should not ignore, either, the fact that in the national energy policy, maybe not in the National Energy Program when announced on a certain date, provision was made for the extension of the natural gas pipeline to eastern Canada, which is an important policy instrument in the West and which permits the surplus of gas which is there in Alberta to be sold to eastern Canada. That is something that many people in my area do not like. It is competition to the advantage of the West. In this case I also think that in the national interest we should have an infrastructure to transmit the gas which is surplus in the West to eastern Canada, to divert away from the nuclear, divert away from oil generation and to try to obtain access to this very efficient, cost-wise, gas resource which comes from Alberta.
Therefore, the Hon. Member should not ignore that there are aspects of the NEP which are not negative. Concerning the Alberta interest, there are provisions in the energy policy of the Government in the area of energy which are also of great advantage to the West now and for the future. I name the southern portion of the Alaska pipeline as another one.
I would just urge these Hon. Members, at some time, to temper their partisanship and to recognize when these things are done, because some of their constituents believe that everything the Government does in the energy area is negative to the West. For the future of the country, I am just urging them to please recognize the advantages and benefits of the policies when they are beneficial to the West.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Mazankowski:
That this House rejects the centralizing and interventionist policies of the Government as an ideologoical thrust aimed at introducing socialization of the Canadian economy by the back door and without the authorization of Parliament, and a definite and present threat to the freedom of Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I hope the Hon. Member for Gloucester (Mr. Breau) does not leave the House too soon because I find it most startling to see how that interventionist stance and that type of thinking is so insensitive to the havoc being wreaked in this country to the point at which the Hon. Member, presumably in a very partisan, supportive way of his Government, stands up here in the House and says that he is proud of the Government. I can understand, for reasons of loyalty or Party discipline, that the Hon. Member maybe feels he cannot speak too openly in criticism of his Government, but it really startles me to hear the Hon. Member say that he is proud of the Government's record.
Let me state for the record the record to which he is referring. For example, in 1968, we had a period of rising inflation to the point at which it rose to 4 per cent. That was the inflation level the year the emperor First took power in this country and introduced his interventionist, socialistic policies about which I want to speak. Thanks to the direction and support of the socialists to my left calling themselves the New Democratic Party, we know that that level of inflation rose to the height of 12.5 per cent in 1981 and was 10.8 per cent last year. Is that the record that the Member for Gloucester says he is proud of, to take inflation from 4 per cent to 10.8 per cent?
With respect to real growth, when the emperor took power in 1968 it was 5.8 per cent. Last year it was negative 4.8 per cent. Is that the record that he is proud of? According to the OECD, that 4.8 per cent put this nation twenty-fourth out of 24 among the major industrialized nations on which the OECD reports. We were behind Iceland in terms of our real growth last year. For example, Turkey's real growth was 5 per cent, which is roughly what we had before the emperor took power in Canada. Turkey had that growth last year, but thanks to the Government whose record this Member is so proud of, we had a negative 4.8 per cent.
Let us look at unemployment. The unemployment rate was 4.5 per cent before the emperor seized power in Canada through misrepresentation. We now find that the unemployment rate last year was 11 per cent. There were a million and a half Canadians not given an opportunity to work in this country, especially the youth of this nation, thanks to the socialistically inspired Trudeau type of policies that have so throttled the inherent ingenuity that could be called upon to create true wealth in this country had it not been frustrated by the interventionist, socialistic tactics of the Government.
I have spoken in general terms of unemployment. Let us look at more meaningful factors. How many Canadians has the Government inflicted unemployment upon? I have mentioned the number of 1.5 million. Before the emperor took power, there were 358,000 unemployed in this country. We thought that was too high at that time. When the Hon. Member says he is proud of his Government's record, can he honestly stand up and say that his Government had no hand in it and this was a matter just like Canadair that was running out of control? Is he saying that somehow the Government should not be called to task or held responsible for that record? Will he seriously suggest that his Government's spending, which amounted to approximately $12 billion at the federal level in 1968 and is now over $80 billion, had nothing to do with those figures? A deficit that was non-existent when his Government took power is now $25 billion, which is actually over $2 billion a month of deficit financing. Would he suggest that that had nothing to do with those sad figures which I have just put on the record concerning our economic morass at the present time?
More simple messages.

The Hon. Member says more simple messages. That is what I find so fraudulent about the socialistic approach to governing. They create the problems and the complications and then say, lo and behold, that they are now lost in the forest. They want to know how to find a way out to some kind of better prosperity, and there are no simple answers.
The truth is that I would like to suggest that there is a way to a new prosperity in Canada. It is a prosperity that will
June 9, 1983

ensure that our productivity can once again be increased. It would ensure that the private sector would be more inclined to spend money on research and development perhaps to reach the point where we would spend 2 per cent of our Gross National Product on research and development. Before the private sector can get moving, we must once again inspire in it the confidence that the Government of the day will not through interventionist tactics and high taxation that basically frustrate the very thing we want to accomplish for all Canadians, that is, higher prosperity, greater real wealth and, in truth, what freedom is all about, a freedom for them to carry on their business and lives with a minimum of Government intervention.
If the Hon. Member dares, perhaps he will get up and try to rebut what I am saying. He likes to use the emperor's classic excuse for the problems with which he now finds himself confronted.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I regret to interrupt the Hon. Member. I believe that the rules are very clear that when any Member of the House is referred to we must refer either to his title, such as if he is a Minister, or to his constituency. The Member has been repeatedly referring to a term, obviously referring to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), which I believe is against the rules.

speechtext: In the opinion of the Chair, the rules are very clear that one should not refer to another Hon. Member by his given or family name. Member, in the Chair s opinion it is parliamentary as long as it is not included in the list of unparliamentary language.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I am sure that you and all Members of the House noted how quickly the Hon. Member associated his Prime Minister with the word "emperor". That clearly meant something to him. He almost automatically assumed that if I was referring to an emperor it was, in truth, the Prime Minister of Canada.
I am very anxious to put on the record what I feel would be some concrete policy moves on the part of the Government of the day that would lead us back to a more free and more private enterprise oriented system. In turn, it would be a system that would produce the jobs and prosperity that this Government is obviously incapable of engendering in Canada at the present time.
I say this because I noticed that, in a classic socialist debating stance, the Hon. Member for Comox-Power River (Mr. Skelly) stood up and spoke in that righteous tone that they like to take to talk about how they have listened to our criticism of the Government but were somehow unable to discern what policy moves we in the Official Opposition would make if we had an opportunity to govern this country. Every socialist has made that kind of argument to some extent. I have noticed that when the Members of the NDP feel that their ally, the present Liberal Party in power, is under attack, they are the
Supply
first to rise to their defence. They try to convey the message that the issue we are talking about is a little more complicated than it is in reality.
In short, let me suggest to that Hon. Member that he might, for example, if he is looking for policy moves, consider a move in which the investment tax credit up to perhaps 10 per cent could be allowed on all investments by the private sector with respect to new investment in manufacturing and non-manufacturing activities. I would suggest that the Member might consider a 5 per cent reduction in the federal corporate income tax rate in order to give industry a somewhat better after tax profit, which is really capital to invest and begin developing our country.
I would like to suggest to the Hon. Member that he take a look at the November, 1981 budget to which presumably they had little objection. That budget changed the capital consumption on manufactured investment, which I think should have been restored to what it was. In other words, if you make an investment prior to the year's end, you could write that investment off 100 per cent. You are allowed only a 50 per cent write-off at the present time.
I would like that Hon. Member to consider that there be various research and development incentives designed to encourage the private sector to increase R and D expenditures combined with any university R and D expenditures and related expenditures in order to reach a target of 2 per cent of the nation's Gross National Product by 1990. That would be in sharp contrast to the 1.1 per cent share we are now putting into research and development in Canada, which is one of the lowest ratios of any industrialized country in the world. Over the next six years that would involve a $20.5 billion incremental. I want to emphasize that extra investment in research and development in Canada.
I would suggest the Hon. Member might take a look, speaking about energy, at a $20 billion energy investment plan to ensure that a marketable surplus exists in oil and gas by 1990. These investments would include additional exploration and development expenditures, several small scale oil sands projects that would produce heavy oil and asphalt type of tar for export markets and, finally, it would provide for the accelerated development of such fields as Hibernia and the Beaufort Sea projects. That is the type of private initiative where the Government essentially sets, if you like, the atmosphere and gives the incentives that we need in Canada in order to get us moving again. What is so encouraging, Mr. Speaker, is that if we started to take those kinds of thrusts we would be able, in the export field alone, if we simply regained the fair share of the world trade market that we used to have prior to the emperor's taking power, to increase our agricultural exports to the rest of the world by $11 billion by 1990. Once again, percentage wise, we would be exporting what we used to export to the rest of the world prior to the emperor's taking over. I would suggest that the type of energy thrusts to which I
COMMONS DEBATES________________ June 9, 1983
Supply
referred would enable further exports of oil and gas to the extent of, say, one hundred million barrels of oil and a comparable amount of gas which, in turn, would strengthen our dollar, lower inflation as a result of that, and which, in turn, would lower the interest rate structure to which we have become accustomed. In short, the creation of jobs would begin.
Let me be more specific. I think the next question which the Hon. Member for Comox-Powell River might ask is, what would be the effect if we did those things we are talking about? Perhaps even the Member for Gloucester would like to know what his Finance Department could tell him if he asked, "Assume we did some of the things to which the Hon. Member for York-Peel (Mr. Sinclair) is referring, what would it do for Canada and the economy between now and 1990?" I think the Hon. Member would find out that it would reduce our inflation level to 4.2 per cent, and it would create 520,000 extra jobs between now and 1990. In short, the trend line on which the last budget of this Government put us was for the creation of 1.4 million jobs in Canada. As we know, that is barely enough to keep unemployment at its present level.
The program I am outlining, according to the respected Data Resources of Canada group, would create 520,000 extra jobs or would create, in contrast to the Government program of 1.4 million jobs, 1.9 million jobs and bring unemployment in this country down to 5.7 per cent by 1990.
I refer to these things only to whet the appetite of Members of this House as to the tremendous potential we have in Canada if we would clear our minds of that socialist cobweb type of thinking which has become parasitical and has basically distracted us from the creation of wealth simply through the building of more and more bureaucracy and more and more Government involvement in all of our lives.
Let me tell you about other things. What I have described would trigger a balanced budget, certainly on a current expenditure basis by 1987. It would basically take us out of any deficit by 1990 and, most important, it would mean, in sharp contrast to the about $20 million of added net debt which the Government plans between now and 1990, that we would be able to reduce that net debt by $44 billion between now and 1990.
The program to which I am referring is a program of only one that could be offered, based on private sector involvement, to give us back some prosperity, some job-creation with less inflation and more real growth. As far as I am concerned, and I would suggest that most Members in my caucus believe Canada deserves better government than it has been getting with the interventionist socialistic alliance that has ruled this country almost without interruption since 1968. It is time we discarded the worn out thinking of these Karl Marx type of people, put back into place what had built the country initially and gave us a hard rock prosperity, namely the private enterprise system built on freedom for all Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member picked up on my words about the expression of my pride. He related that to things other than what I said. Just in case the interpretation
did not come to him clearly, I was talking about the unprecedented evolution in the last 15 years with regard to the introduction of legislation and the enshrinement in the Constitution of language rights, fundamental rights and basic rights. This is what I was talking about. I would think that even the Hon. Member, sometimes as partisan as he is, would recognize that.
When the Hon. Member refers to this Government as being socialistic, interventionist and against business, I ask, how can he really say that honestly when in the last budget five changes were brought to the investment tax credit to lengthen the period in which industries could claim it from five years to 11 years in some cases? We have introduced, for example, the concept of the equity holder being able, in some circumstances, to claim the tax credit if the investor or the company cannot claim it. He knows the investment tax credit was proposed by a Liberal Government, not a Conservative Government. How can he say that this Government does not look to encourage business where it can when we brought in these five changes in the last budget to the investment tax credit? For example, this may permit Noranda Mines to obtain the equity it needs when the market improves to build a zinc reduction plant in New Brunswick. Instead of the provincial or Federal Government's doing it, we are providing a tax regime in which equity holders and the company will be able to do it. How can the Hon. Member say such things when such beneficial changes were made to the investment tax credit in the last budget?

Mr. Speaker, I would like to respond to the two comments of the Hon. Member for Gloucester. First he indicated that somehow I had taken out of context his reference to being proud of the Government's record, and also he referred to such things as enshrinement of various rights. Here again I think it shows how the Hon. Member is totally insensitive to what the Government has done to the average Canadian. The average Canadian cannot eat the enshrinement of some type of paper reference in a document such as the one to which the Hon. Member referred. The average Canadian wants work. The average Canadian is denied jobs, jobs, jobs. I suggest that it is the Government's fundamental obligation to meet the right of every Canadian to a meaningful job. That is the right which the Government has taken away with its interventionist, socialistic approaches.
Then, in typical Liberal fashion, chameleonlike, he turned around and said, "How can you say that we are unfriendly with business?" It has absolutely beaten business into the ground, particularly the oil and gas industry. Then Government Members turn around and say, "Instead of hitting you 100 times, we will hit you 95 times next year. Are you not pleased that we have laid back on five?"
In short, the Government must be looked at in light of the over-all thrust of what it has done since 1968. John Turner and the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) cannot deny the record. That is their legacy to Canada. The Government of Canada has taken an interventionist, socialistic approach
June 9, 1983

which has been demonstrated not to work by the fact that we are now ranked twenty-fourth out of 24 OECD nations. That is what I am speaking to.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to correct and comment on some of the things the Hon. Member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens) said. First, I said that the Conservative Party refused to put on record its policies and procedures. I note for the record that the Hon. Member for York-Peel has never been too abashed to do that. We have noted his approach to the problems in El Salvador and Central America, which I would say was in support of the governments in power there and the very nefarious activities going on.
We know that the Hon. Member for York-Peel is on the far right of the Conservative Party. He mentioned three points in terms of expanding the oil industry, but the additional expenditures would be simply the trickle down effect where we pay the companies and the wealthy and hope that it trickles through. He suspects that the freeing up of $20 billion will get things rolling, but it will simply serve to engorge multinational oil companies in Canada. Speeding up Hibernia and Beaufort Sea explorations cannot be done in the face of declining world oil prices. His proposal to export 100 million barrels of oil will simply deprive Canadians now and in the future of an opportunity of access to light crude. Basically it is an absolutely ridiculous approach to the solution of problems in Canada.
I want to admit that I was mistaken on one matter. The Hon. Member for York-Peel, in a different way than most other Members of the Conservative Party, put on the record proposals which I think would be very seriously looked at in terms of an election.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to respond to the comments of the Hon. Member for Comox-Powell River which reflect how out of touch he and the New Democratic Party are. The British have spoken today. They have given a massive vote of support for Margaret Thatcher and her Conservative policies in the United Kingdom. There is a wave in the world today in favour of conservatism and diametrically opposed to the socialistic, dogmatic type of approach which perhaps was in vogue in the 1960s. The socialistic approach is out of favour. This is reflected also by the results of today's Gallup poll that showed our friends to my left have now fallen back to a mere 16 per cent of popular support.
1 understand how Members of the New Democratic Party feel. They are a little fluttery at the present time as they sense how the world is passing them by. If the Hon. Member wants to see some action in the House, if he wants to see jobs for Canadians, and if he wants to see less inflation and lower interest rates, he will hae an opportunity very shortly to allow us to form the new Government after the next election. We will put some truly free enterprise oriented policies back into vogue and allow Canadians to create some prosperity once again without a leechlike Public Service oriented Government living off their backs.
Message from the Senate

Mr. Speaker, as I listened to the Hon. Member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens), it sounded very familiar. It sounded like the program which the presidential candidate of the Republican Party, Mr. Reagan, proposed three years ago. The Americans, as they had the right under democracy, accepted his argument. Three years down the road and after the United States Government did the kinds of things the Hon. Member for York-Peel has been advocating, such as cutting taxes to the business community, giving greater incentives and the rest of it, Americans are still faced with over 10 per cent unemployment.
I would like to ask him a specific question. He talked about the deficit. Of course we have a large deficit. A substantial part of it was brought about by the very large increase in transfer payments which the federal Government pays to the Provinces for post-secondary education, hospital insurance and medical insurance. If there is a Conservative Government in the future of which he is a Minister-and that is a very unlikely possibility-and if it is faced with a large deficit, would it cut back on transfer payments, particularly for programs such as hospital insurance, medical insurance, old age pensions and family allowances?

Aren't they beautiful, Mr. Speaker? They always come up with that old bogey that the only way we can get back to prosperity and reduce the deficit in the country is by cutting back their precious spending programs. The fact is that with what I outlined we would not have to cut from the real growth in federal Government expenditures one five-cent piece. All we would do is to put some faith back into the private sector and let it do the job of creating the wealth, which in turn will create the tax revenue we need to start balancing the budget.
If I could comment on one other matter, the Hon. Member referred to the program in the United States. He might be interested in a contrast between what has happened in Canada and what has happened in the United States in the last five years. The real Gross National Product in Canada went up 13 per cent, whereas in the United States it went up 19 per cent, and in every other economic aspect we did worse.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Mazankowski:
That this House rejects the centralizing and interventionist policies of the Government as an ideological thrust aimed at introducing socialization of the Canadian economy by the back door and without the authorization of Parliament, and a definite and present threat to the freedom of Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, if I can say at the outset and if you can believe it, having listened to the Hon. Member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens), I still get some pleasure from listening to the Hon. Member. It is one of the few consistent things in this ever-revolving world. He has not changed since he crawled on a kiddy-car some decades ago. He is still riding on the far rightwing of the highway. He has been on the gravel he first walked and talked.
It must be a nostalgic moment for the Hon. Member because tomorrow night a number of his colleagues will be facing off in the political forum of their Party for the leadership, and this time around he is not there. A Member from the NDP said a moment ago that the Hon. Member for York-Peel was on the right wing of the Party. That may be how it was seven years ago in the leadership campaign, but now he is right in the centre of the Conservative Party, far over on the right wing of the highway, about to fall off in the abyss. The Canadian people certainly will not buy that kind of right-wing extremism. Still it is great to see the Hon. Member steady on course and basically out of tune with the mainstream of the Canadian public.
Let's try an election.

His voice is strong, as his determination is strong. Might I also add that he made mention a moment ago of the elections in Great Britain. Remember, something has changed in Great Britain. The fact is that there are two major Opposition Parties. There are far more people opposed to the Government of Great Britain in Great Britain today than there are supporting that Government, thank goodness.
The reason why I wish to speak this afternoon is simply that I want to respond to comments made this morning by the Hon. Member for Wellington Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Beatty). It has been quite a while since I have had a chance to rise in this House and speak in debate because I have had few, if any opportunities to address myself to my portfolio. That may mean that I am doing everything right, and Members of the Opposition, particularly the Official Opposition, see that there is nothing to criticize. I would be delighted if that were the
case. At any rate, I am glad to have a chance this afternoon to respond what I find to be absolutely incredible rhetoric put forward by the Hon. Member for Wellington-Dufferin-Simcoe this morning.
Politics is a natural adversarial system. We stand up and each of us, depending on what Party we are in, do our very best to present in the best possible light our point of view. I must say that the Hon. Member for Wellington-Dufferin-Simcoe did not do justice to himself, his Party, his credibility or his Party's credibility by taking the track he followed this morning. The Canadian public is fed up with hyperbole, and it was nothing but hyperbole today, a clear distortion of any of the facts involved in the Government's proposal on how to deal with concentration of ownership in the Canadian newspaper industry.
The speech this morning was a classic example of the Official Opposition throughout this Parliament: bereft of any policy of its own, full of nothing but negativisms about anybody else's suggestions. That is not very healthy for any democracy. It is an exchange of ideas so that the public can determine largely what it would best accept.
The Hon. Member for Wellington-Dufferin-Simcoe began this morning by saying that with these proposals concerning the daily newspaper industry in Canada we were threatening even the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, that our proposals were an attack on the basic freedoms of Canadians and that today there is less freedom in Canada than there was in 1968. Other Members before me outlined how ridiculous that charge is. I want to respond specifically to a couple of points, distortions or whatever that Member made this morning.
The Hon. Member said that the Government had raided a newspaper, that no other Government in history had done that. It is not a very palatable thing to have any newspaper raided. I am a former journalist. I wish to give a small reminder of the facts rather than the distortions. The Royal Canadian Mounted Police raided a newspaper. It did so because it thought there was secret information that might jeopardize the wellbeing of Canada. They may have been wrong, they may have been right, but it was the Royal Canadian Mounted Police which recommended and then acted on that. It is a very serious thing ever to intrude upon freedom of the press by any authority of Government, but clearly the security of the state is worth considering, rather than the kind of rhetoric of the Hon. Member, which seemed to suggest that no matter what a newspaper might do at any time to deal with that. You must have a right to deal with that and the Canadian public will judge whether you dealt with it appropriately.
The Hon. Member said that this Government had developed a propaganda war chest to serve its own purposes and to give misinformation to the public. That is ironic. That comes from a Member who was a Minister in the Clark Government, who set up a system under which, in order to decide what advertising firm would work for the Government and where the Government's advertisements would be placed, it would hire a small group of its friends and do it away from Government,
June 9, 1983

away from the scrutiny of Parliament. They would decide who the advertisers would be and who in turn would get the advertisements. Therefore, that was a pretty hollow attack.
Let me get to the basic nonsense we heard about the Government's proposals on the daily newspapers in Canada and increasing concentration of ownership. The Hon. Member said it was a new assault on freedom of the press in Canada, it was legislation to regulate ownership, it would affect the ability of the press to do its job. He said that anything Government does is calculated for self-interest. He said Government will control the ability of organizations to run their newspapers.
What are we proposing? We are simply saying that at the current time in Canada in English language daily newspapers there are two very large newspaper chains that control approximately 60 per cent of all of the daily newspapers' circulation. What is freedom of the press if not our proposals to limit concentration from going any further? Surely freedom of the press is as much freedom from Government intrusion in the newsroom as freedom from monetary power, allowing people to have access to a diversity of views.
Surely competition is essential to a free press. If increasingly there are fewer and fewer owning more and more of our daily press, there is less of a challenge of accuracy in direct competition. There is less ability for senior journalists to move about in the job if what they want to tell or say is suppressed by management. There is less ability for Canadians to be sure that they are getting a diversity of view rather than a diversity of one or two publishers or owners who control most of the newspapers in the country.
What is the real threat? The real threat to freedom of the press in Canada is that money power will allow for a lack of any law and too much in the hands of too few. Were a Government not to act, that would be irresponsible. Let me add something else that I think is irresponsible.
In all the questions during Question Period and all the charges about the Government attacking the freedom of the press in Canada, never once-and this will surprise no one- did the Hon. Member from the Official Opposition suggest what he would do. Is he simply here as the "houseboy" of the publishers, or does he have a view? Does he think there should be more concentration? Do we have a free press if two companies own all the English language daily newspapers in the country? Is that what he would like? Is concentration of ownership not a problem?
It amuses me because it shows how far to the right they have gone. When every publisher or representative of the owners of daily newspapers in this country has told me over two years of consultation that concentration of ownership can be a problem-they will not say at what level but they admit it is a problem-the Official Opposition still will not admit it can be a problem or admit what is their position. Would it be a free press if they did nothing and more and more fell into the hands of fewer and fewer and there was no diversity and no competition? That is hardly responsible policy.
Supply
The next charge was that we were going to set up a press council and that it would have its first chairman and vicechairman appointed by the Government, that it would be a convenient vehicle for Government to interfere any time it chooses, that the single greatest threat to a free press is a Government sitting in judgment of the free press, and that is what we see today with this proposal for a press council.
Let me tell you about the press council. That is all untrue. Either the Hon. Member cannot read or he has no willingness to talk about the facts. The fact is the membership of the press council, as set down in the proposed law, would have publishers' representatives and journalists' representatives in balanced numbers, in fair numbers from all of the five regions. They together would choose representatives from the general public with no conflict within the newspaper industry. None of them would be appointed. They would make the decisions and the balance of voting power would be with the public's representatives when hearing complaints. How is that Government interference in the press? It is not. To be sure, Government will not interfere but, to be sure, people have the right to vent their concerns, especially since almost all major cities in Canada, with the exception of three or four, have only one major newspaper. Those daily newspapers have a monopoly. The written word has a certain power, and I and many other Canadians and the Government think that individual Canadians and groups of Canadians deserve the right to have the ability to complain if they feel they are not being treated properly by a monopoly daily newspaper with all its power of print.
We are saying to the press that if they do not get credible press councils going, the Government will set up the framework of a council. The members of the press will determine their own workload, they will decide who the representatives will be from publishers and journalists, who are not always friendly with one another, and, as I said earlier, there will be the public's representatives holding the balance of power.
Now, Mr. Speaker, how does that illustrate the phrase, "the single greatest threat to a free press is a Government sitting in judgment of a free press"? How does that illustrate the phrase, "a convenient vehicle for Government to interfere any time it chooses"? That kind of rhetoric totally distorts the reality of the proposal and does not lead to productive debate on this focal point of Canadian democracy but makes democracy unproductive. I think that that is very irresponsible.
Once more, where is that Member who is the Party's critic? Where is that Party that, as the Official Opposition, says that it will form the next Government? Members of the Official Opposition can tell us what is wrong. They can distort and twist the facts of the matter, but they cannot tell us what their own position is.
The next charge laid by the Hon. Member was a document that indicated that advisers on the Government side said that what we want to do would be illegal, especially with reference to the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission reviewing

June 9, 1983

possible newspaper purchases and start-ups by companies that are largely engaged in other businesses. We do not need a lawyer to tell us that the federal Government has the right to review anything. There may well be a question as to whether the Government has the right to impose penalties or laws because there are split jurisdictions, but the Government does have the right to review anything, and that is all that is proposed.
The Government proposes to make the point with the public that a company which is engaged largely in other areas should not reach into the newsroom so that the newsroom loses its independence by being fearful of criticizing the other areas that the parent company is involved in. Once more, that was a major concern of the Kent Commission, and I think that it is something that a lot of Canadians are worried about as well, especially when so much of the daily newspaper circulation is in the hands of so few.
The Hon. Member then went on to say that he had requested the Library of Parliament to prepare a research paper that said that there are serious doubts about the federal Government's jurisdiction. He then went to quote what those doubts were, but they all related to the Kent Commission. Indeed, that is exactly what I said when I announced the Government's proposals. With every good intention, we found those proposals either too intrusionary, appearing to be too intrusionary, or both, into the newsrooms. Government politicians should not enter the newsrooms. They have no right to be there. That is why our proposals are as limited as they are and as passive as they are. They set parameters for review or turn over to others the responsability of review with no input from us.
But we cannot have it both ways. We rejected the Kent proposals in part because of jurisdictional problems as well as the others I have just mentioned. If the Hon. Member's document says that, then he simply agrees with us. What we propose and what we will soon have in draft form is an Act that is legal as far as our lawyers are concerned and is very important to a free press in Canada.
As he wound up, the Hon. Member said that we were going to ram this through the House. The rhetoric really does get tiresome. We are going to ram it through the House? The Royal Commission met for a year and then brought forward its findings. I consulted with everybody I possibly could consult with for eight or nine months. Then we made our proposals and I have consulted on them for one year. When the proposals come to Parliament, I have indicated that I want them to be in Parliament and I want any proposals in the form of an Act. I do not want anything to be done by regulation or Order in Council because it is a sensitive area, and I want it fully vented and discussed in committee. Although I have said that publicly, the Hon. Member says that that is ramming it through the House.
Do you know what will probably happen when we have that legislation, Mr. Speaker? The Hon. Member and a handful of his friends will hold it up and hold it up on second reading and say that we are ramming it through the House, when all we are trying to do is to get it to committee so that other Canadians can discuss it. Mark my words. See if that is not what
happens. Mr. Speaker, I will bet that he still does not have a policy at that time that will deal with what can be done to protect the free press from the danger that is created when too much is in the hands of too few.
Finally, the Hon. Member said that these proposals contained shades of Orwell's "1984" and were only measures to make the press beholden to Government. He said that owners of Newspapers will have to win the favour of Government. He did not tell us how that would be done, because there is no way that we suggest that that would have to be the case. We have set parameters and there is no retroactivity for those who are already beyond the 20 per cent threshold in concentration of ownership. It is the meekest, mildest, most limited package that can be imagined simply because, as a former journalist myself, 1 do not believe we can do anything that would appear to be intrusionary. At worst, we offer grants for better interregional coverage and better coverage from abroad by people knowledgeable about Canada. That is a passive intrusion, one with no judgments, one that is on a first come, first served basis if there is no bureau in place already. Nobody is obligated to take the money if he does not want to take the money.
The Hon. Member concluded that the whole nefarious proposal was an attempt by the Government to shackle the free press which he said is so important to a democracy. Well, let me say that if Members of his Party were in charge, their inaction would shackle the democracy in an area vital to a competitive free press. Their inaction would allow conglomerates perhaps to use their influence to have the press make sure only their story got out. I would like to believe that conglomerate ownerships and large companies operate largely with goodwill within Canada, but they operate for their own interest and for their own profit line.
Surely Parliament must set limits at times that will protect a democracy and allow for diversity. We have proposed a law that will allow for that diversity and that will limit competition. We have proposed a review that will encourage editorial independence. We have proposed that in any individual marketplace, there should be no cross media ownership because there must be competition if there are to be facts and accuracy and diversity. We have proposed that there should be better inter-regional coverage in Canada and better coverage of Canadian interests abroad. When so many major cities only have one daily newspaper, we have proposed that individual Canadians should have a way to grieve if they feel that that powerful instrument has not been fair to them. I do not know how anybody can argue that any of that does anything but protect a free press, and a free press really means the rights of individuals to a diversity of sources of information.
Where are Members of the Official Opposition on this policy? They are nowhere. Who are they? They are friends of big business and, apparently, the newspaper conglomerates. What are they? Apparently they are destroyers of legitimate and rational debate and policy production.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Comments, questions? Are there any question or comments? Debate.

June 9, 1983

Mr. Speaker, the resolution before us today is an incredible piece of chicanery. Unfortunately, the only reason it tends to stick is that there is some shred of truth to it. I would like to use the ten minutes remaining to build on some of the remarks made by the Hon. Member for Gloucester (Mr. Breau) about the performance of the Government that gives a shred of credibility and truth to resolutions such as we see before the House today.
I would like to use as an example a small community in British Columbia that suffers because of the nature of Government intervention and the lack of what I would call the effectiveness of Government. Alert Bay is a small community on an island that sits at the head of Johnstone Strait. It encompasses 2,000 people, approximately 1,000 people who live in a native community and 1,000 people who live in an adjoining community. This community hangs in a life and death balance, Mr. Speaker, and that life and death balance is influenced on almost a daily basis by the Government and how it responds or fails to respond to that community.
When we speak about intervention, we also mean interest and understanding and communication. These things do not exist in Alert Bay. The Government is 3,000 miles away. It has no interest in the community, and consequently the community has no interest in the Government.
The present Government wonders why it has no representation from western Canada. Maybe the explanation that will follow will assist it in developing appropriate intervention which supports the kind of personal and private initiative that we would like to see, the kind of intervention that enhances the independence of the community to make decisions which affect their day to day lives and, in short, gives people independence.
I am sorry that the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) left the Chamber, Mr. Speaker, because his Department has great influence on what happens in that community through unemployment insurance and the employment development process. Alert Bay does get some recognition, but there are tremendous problems with the delivery of unemployment insurance in the community. When you combine that with the inefficiency of the post office, Alert Bay, like many communities in rural and remote Canada, suffers tremendously. People judge that it is suffering at the hands of the Department that comes under the Minister of Employment and Immigration as well as at the hands of the Government. Tremendous difficulties are imposed upon it.
Banking is a federal responsibility and Alert Bay has no bank. It has a small credit union on which the local business community is absolutely dependent. The small businesses that are trying to survive and grow in the community are dependent on a credit union that is hanging in there by a thread. By failing to intervene in some of the problems of the credit union, that sole source of banking in the community, the federal Government puts the small businesses in the community in jeopardy. Debts are incurred in areas of federal responsibility where the credit union could be made more viable and stronger and could serve the needs of the people more effectively. I urge
Supply
the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Cosgrove) to look at the problems in the community.
Indian affairs is another area of concern. With approximately 1,000 people in the native community the Nimpkish band is struggling for economic development, for access to the forest industry, for appropriate intervention in the fishing industry, for development of their culture and the education of their children. The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Munro) is a long way from Alert Bay. There are many and serious problems with employment and economic development that affect the day to day life of the native people and the opportunity for them to earn a living in order to support themselves and their children. The Government wonders why the people in that community and in all of western Canada reject that Party as a source of representation in the House.
I am pleased to see that the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. De Bane) is in the House. The Johnstone Strait fishery is one of the most complex in western Canada, yet it is the people of Alert Bay and Sointula and the area at the head of Johnstone Strait that depend, absolutely and desperately, on income from the fishing industry. Every fish caught in Johnstone Strait by a fisherman from Alert Bay, from the Nimpkish band, from Port Hardy, from Sointula, is a ten dollar bill in those small communities. Every fish is the lifeblood of those communities. Yet the officials in the field decided to let the fish swim by and be taken elsewhere at a lower value. That put Alert Bay on the slippery skids to oblivion. There is a question of understanding that community and its dependence on that resource. The Government must understand this and extend aid to the community.
On the matter of small craft harbours, I must point out that the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans has had in his possession for seven years a request for harbour development. Alert Bay contains one of the largest fishing harbours in the area. The largest number of fishing boats on the West Coast is in that area. Seven years ago they made a request to build a fishing harbour there, but it has been ignored. As a matter of fact, harbour developments have been placed in communities that have no fishing harbour. Some of the communities that have received benefits do not even have major vessels harboured there. I suggest that this is so critical that if the fishing vessels are drained away from Alert Bay, it will kill the community. It is vitally important that the Government understand this. If that should happen, at least the people of Alert Bay should be informed. I hope the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans will take note of this and respond to it.
Another problem is transportation. There is a Coast Guard communications system which involves five or six people at a Coast Guard radio station. The Minister proposes to remove them from that community and put in a remote station which will remote to Vancouver. This is a compromise with safety. Those radio operators know the area like the back of their hand and when there is an emergency, they know who is closest and able to respond and exactly where that person is.

When this is remoted to Vancouver, the local operator there has no more detailed knowledge of the area than he has of Timbuktu. The proposal to remote that Coast Guard radio station is dangerous and it will erode the economic viability of the community. It is imperative that the Minister of Communications (Mr. Fox) have his officials talk to the people of the community about this. They should also talk to the other Government Departments involved so that there is a complete understanding not only of what is happening in the community but of how each Department affects the life, growth, hope and expectations of the people.
Also, the Department of the Solicitor General intervenes in the community without understanding it. An RCMP boat is involved in law enforcement and search and rescue. It is greatly respected in the community. It is often quite dangerous on the water with the tremendous traffic involved in the fishing industry, the ferries intersecting, the major marine routes for ocean going freighters, and the RCMP play an effective role there. In the past, the Solicitor General's office has proposed that the five officers involved be moved out of the community. That has not happened to date but it would have a bad effect if it did.
In the past, the Department of Fisheries and Oceans has attempted to remove the fisheries office where some of the most difficult fishing management decisions are made. If those officers are removed from Alert Bay, communications will break down and the economy will be eroded.
There is a desperate need for Government Departments that intervene in the community and whose goals and aspirations, we hope, are to allow the community to thrive and continue to grow, to begin to talk to each other about the nature of the community and how they can help. They should then begin to talk to the community about where it wants to go. That is absolutely imperative.
At the present time we have a Senator who roams the coast of British Columbia. Instead of establishing priorities and discussing with the people of the communities how the Government will intervene and become involved in the day to day lives of people in a meaningful way so that they can make decisions themselves to secure their future, he comes out and announces where the small craft harbour will go, by total surprise. He comes out and announces where the salmon enhancement projects will go, by total surprise to the people of the communities.
Through the intervention of Cabinet Ministers an interdepartmental committee must be set up to study the needs of the area, to consult with the people and look at ways in which the Government can work with them to determine how they can be assisted. In some cases the solution might be for the Government to keep its nose out, but in other cases there are many things that the federal Government can do to assist such communities and help the people to preserve their way of life and make it better.
If the Government is interested in developing a good relationship and not exposing itself to the hot air rhetoric of the
Conservative motion, I offer them these constructive suggestions and a positive course of action that could be used in communities along the whole coast of British Columbia and in many of the remote communities of Canada.

speakerposition: Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: HOUSE OF COMMONS-CANADIAN BILL OF RIGHTS-ABSENCE FROM DISPLAY WITHIN PARLIAMENT BUILDINGS. (B) REQUEST THAT BILL OF RIGHTS BE DISPLAYED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I take part in the Adjournment Debate this evening in an attempt to receive a little more information from the Government on the subject of a question I asked on June 6, 1983, as reported on page 26077 of Hansard.
It was brought to my attention by several constituents when I was showing them through their Parliament Buildings, through the buildings which are an honour, a tribute, and the property of all Canadians, that the Diefenbaker Bill of Rights was not displayed. I was showing them our Library, their Library. In the past I have always made a point of pointing out in the display cases on the desk in the Library the Flag Proclamation which gave Canadians their own flag. I have also pointed out the Diefenbaker Bill of Rights and other documents in the form of statutes of historic importance to Canada and to Candians in the development of our country. To my dismay, however, I could not show them the Diefenbaker Bill of Rights which used to be displayed in either language. It was not available. I looked through the documents in the display in the Hall of Honour which has just been opened in the corridor leading to the Library. There were several documents displayed at that time, which supposedly pertained to the constitutional development of our country, the Acts that have brought us to this point in history.
I would like to enumerate some of those Acts which are in the Hall of Honour, Mr. Speaker. There is the edict creating the Sovereign Council of Quebec, 1663, the Royal Proclamation of 1763, the Quebec Act, 1774, the Constitutional Act, 1791, the Union Act, 1840. There is also the Constitution Act of 1867 which in itself is an anomaly because up until recently that Act has always been called the British North America Act. There was the Canada Act of 1982 and the Proclamation of the Constitution Act, 1982.
June 9, 1983

I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) what had happened to this document, this Statute that when passed by the Parliament of Canada was to be the supreme Statute pertaining to constitutional rights of all Canadians. One of the rights which was in that Constitution Act passed under the Diefen-baker Government, commonly known as the Diefenbaker Bill of Rights, was the right of Canadian citizens to own and to hold property.
In checking to see what had happened to this historic document, I found that in 1967, Centennial Year, the then Prime Minister, Lester Pearson, wished to display to Canadians two important historic Acts. The ones he did display were the Proclamation of the Flag along with the Diefenbaker Bill of Rights, the original of which was displayed for two years, up until 1969. Then through some problems with humidity and some concern for the wellbeing of this important document it was removed. The document was replaced in the display case originally by a unilingual document, which was to be rotated, using one or other of the official languages, on a monthly basis. Shortly after that another display case was built and it was then possible to display it in both English and French. Up until this time, Mr. Speaker, I have not been able to find out, or, even receive a reply from the Government, what really has happened to this document and where it is. This document was the first Bill of Rights in recent history given to the Canadian people. It is a Statute which still remains, and was originally to be pre-eminent over all other documents.
