speakeroldname: Mr. Denis Ethier (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
subtopic: HOUSE OF COMMONS-CANADIAN BILL OF RIGHTS-ABSENCE FROM DISPLAY WITHIN PARLIAMENT BUILDINGS. (B) REQUEST THAT BILL OF RIGHTS BE DISPLAYED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, to mark the patriation of the Canadian Charter the Government of the United Kingdom gave to Canada, on October 1, 1983, facsimilies of the major British documents respecting Canada's constitutional development, including the Royal Proclamation of 1763; the Quebec Act, 1774; the Constitutional Act, 1791; the Union Act, 1840; and the British North America Act, 1867. At the same time, the British Foreign Secretary, Francis Pym, also presented a special copy of the Canada Act 1982, produced on parchment.
The Speaker of the Senate and the Speaker of the House of Commons decided that these documents of Canada's constitutional development should be put on display in the Hall of Honour so that thousands of Canadians who visit Parliament each year might be able to gain an even greater understanding of various stages in the evolution of Canada as a sovereign state.
They also decided that the edict creating the Sovereign Council of Quebec, 1663, which established New France as a royal Province and made provision for civil Government, should figure in the display. That original document is on loan from the Archives of France until September 5, 1983. The collection of documents of Canada's constitutional development also includes the proclamation of the Constitution Act, 1982, signed by Queen Elizabeth II. This document completed Canada's evolution as a fully sovereign state.
The collection of constitutional documents is complemented by a display of three proclamations establishing Canada's symbol of sovereignty: The Royal Proclamation of the Coat of Arms of Canada, 1921; the Proclamation of the Canadian Flag, 1965; and the Proclamation of the National Anthem, "O, Canada", 1980.
The number of documents to be included in such an exhibition is inevitably limited. The main exhibit deals only with the principle documents respecting Canada's constitutional development leading to full sovereignty, and the complementary exhibition deals only with the Canadian symbols of sovereignty. The exhibition of documents does not seek to deal with every aspect of Canada's constitutional and political evolution. For this reason, it was decided that another exhibition dealing with other aspects should be organized by the Public Archives.
I might say at this time that the Public Archives removed this document from the showcase because a signature on the document was being raised by the light reflecting in the
showcase.
It should be noted that the exhibition in the Hall of Honour includes The Proclamation of the Constitution Act, 1982, which brought into force that Act which includes the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. However, the Constitution Act, 1982, itself is not included in the display.

Adjournment Debate
The collection of constitutional documents does not include the many historic statutes of the Parliament of Canada that are of great significance for the people of Canada, such as the Official Languages Act of 1969, or indeed the Canadian Citizenship Act of 1947 or, for that matter, the Canadian Bill of Rights of 1960. The exclusion of such documents does not reflect in any way on their importance for Canadians.

subtopic: RAILWAYS-CROWSNEST PASS RATE-RAILWAY UPGRADING-PRIME MINISTER'S POSITION
RAILWAYS-CROWSNEST PASS RATE-RAILWAY UPGRADING-PRIME MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on May 20 I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) a quesiton concerning the railway upgrading and the Crowsnest pass rate. I was basically attempting to determine from the Prime Minister whether he had been very clear in his discussions with the various provincial Premiers and interest groups in the West when he asked their opinions of his proposed transportation initiatives. 1 asked if he had been clear as to whether he was talking about the need for railway upgrading, and what was their opinion as to the need for that activity, aside from a decision to change the historic Crowsnest rate charged to farmers. He fudged the issue somewhat in his answer.
In his answer as reported at page 25627 of Hansard, he said:
There are two aspects, and some of my interlocutors are more interested in one aspect than in the other. For instance, it is easy to see that those who are interested in an improved transportation system would probably include a lot of Manitobans, because I understand the Minister of Transport has announced or will announce that there will be some 1,000 proper cars or so built at the Transcona plant in Winnipeg.
That was the point on which I wish to raise an interjection. The cars that are being built in Winnipeg have nothing to do with the proposed transportation Bill C-155 that was before the House. Those cars are not being built to transport grain. They will be coal cars and there is a vast difference in the design and utilization, consequently, of those cars.
The cars being built in Winnipeg are small volume cars designed to carry a very dense material like coal. They cannot be interchanged for use in grain haulage and really fall outside the proposed legislation we are being asked to discuss in the House. As well they fall outside the discussions that have been going on between various farm groups and, to some extent, the provincial Premiers.
I believe the Prime Minister's answer left us with the impression that the question of the rate and upgrading were thoroughly and inalterably intertwined. Our Party and many other people in Canada do not see that to be the case, and that view is held not only by western Canadians but by people right across the country.
We have been making the point for some time in the House that the railway's ability to move grain has not really been limited by the amount of technology that exists in the railways now. Railways have upgraded considerably and consistently. Admittedly, they have done so through intrusions into the public purse at times. However, we note that the proposed
June 9, 1983
subsidies included in Bill C-155 of $651 million annually include subsidies that have existed under previous legislation. For example, there is the branch line subsidy of $278 million which is being paid now annually. I would remind the House that those subsidies are being paid to transport the grain directly from the elevator to the seaboard, and they relate to all the costs of moving grain from those branch lines directly to the seaboard. That covers closeto 30 per cent or 35 per cent of the total crop moved in the country.
I think there are some problems regarding the background reasoning for the decision that has been made. Let me point out a couple of things. The railways cannot obtain more efficiency with this rate. The rate was very profitable up until the last 15 or 20 years. There is some dispute as to whether or not it is still profitable. Many figures we have been able to obtain would indicate that the railways come very close to covering all their operating costs. The upgrading costs are being paid out of the public purse. The cost of the hopper cars is being paid out of the public purse, from farmers pockets and with provincial money.
As far as efficiency of the railways is concerned, using one format for computing efficiency, this has gone from roughly a train load average of 22 cars at the beginning of the century to a situation today when 110 cars are moved per train load. The cars today are much larger than the ones used in 1900. The efficiency ratio there is about ten times in terms of the crew and backup people necessary to maintain the trains on the tracks. About one-fifth of the crews and backup staff are now needed if you compute efficiency on a train load basis.
If you compute efficiency on a tonne mile basis, about one-fiftieth of the backup staff is needed today compared with the turn of the century. Costs are not consistent with what occurred back then.
There have been many ways of reducing costs. The compensatory rate Mr. Snavely determined is not very accurate. When you use his figures and superimpose them on the financial statement for one of the most profitable years of CPR you will find, on a train load basis, that the returns would be more than twice the actual train load mile costs.
We argue that the Prime Minister has not fully understood the problem. It is not just an economic problem, it is a social problem. It is a problem affecting the security of the country as an economic entity. It is a regional problem, not just an economic problem. It is a truly political problem of a national sense. I again call upon the Minister to split the Bill, split the two issues and deal with them as two separate issues, which they most clearly are.

speakeroldname: Mr. Denis Ethier (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
subtopic: RAILWAYS-CROWSNEST PASS RATE-RAILWAY UPGRADING-PRIME MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) well understands the situation. The question is whether railway upgrading and changing the Crow rate are
June 9, 1983

inseparable issues. It is the Government's view that the two must go together. Theoretically, I suppose it would be possible to charge arbitrarily low freight rates for certain commodities, and then to pour taxpayers' money into upgrading whenever it is thought to be needed. But in the Government's view, it is neither sound management nor sound economics to charge freight rates that bear no relationship to the costs incurred in the transportation.
Grain is perhaps the only commodity in the country in respect of which 4025;-1 freight rate bear no relationship to transportation costs. Rail freight rates for other commodities, elevator charges, passenger fares on public transit, even public utility fees-for example, Manitoba Hydro, in a Province with an NDP Government-have been subject to periodic fee increases in an attempt to recover a reasonable proportion of the cost incurred. Unless there is a reasonable amount of revenue from each type of traffic, it becomes impossible to determine whether that traffic will grow or decrease, where it will move and, consequently, where investment for upgrading of facilities are required.
None of the above excludes Government support of grain transportation, even as a long run proposition. The Government fully recognizes the contribution of grain to Canada's exports and balance of payments. That is why grain will never have to pay the full cost of transportation. Under the present plan, it will pay about 60 per cent of the true cost by 19901991. If grain prices remain depressed, the "safety net" will take effect before that and grain will pay a smaller proportion of transportation costs.
The Government is convinced that some additional revenue is required from grain to allow the railways to commit themselves to the expansion needed to accommodate future growth in traffic over the next decade.

subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-REQUEST THAT CF-104 AIRCRAFT BE BANNED FROM AEROBATIC DEMONSTRATIONS. (B) REQUEST FOR DOCUMENTATION ON ACCIDENTS
NATIONAL DEFENCE-REQUEST THAT CF-104 AIRCRAFT BE BANNED FROM AEROBATIC DEMONSTRATIONS. (B) REQUEST FOR DOCUMENTATION ON ACCIDENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to elaborate on a question I asked some time ago in the House concerning the Canadian Armed Forces operation of the CF-104. Of the 239 acquired by the Canadian Armed Forces, 110 have crashed and there has been a 46 per cent failure rate. Over the last six months five pilots have been killed in CF-104 accidents, and over the term of its use approximately 33 have been killed.
When the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Lamontagne) was questioned about this in the House, he indicated that the Opposition was attempting to make a tragedy out of the most recent situation in Germany in which a clergyman and his family were killed by the crash of a CF-104, with a greater tragedy just narrowly being missed with thousands of people watching an Armed Forces public display.
There is no doubt in anyone's mind that this is an extremely dangerous aircraft. It was pointed out that some squadrons in the RAF had better flight safety records and less loss of
Adjournment Debate
aircraft during the second world war when the aircraft were actually involved in active combat than the CF-104. The aircraft seems to have some design problems. It is a single engine aircraft which cannot be relit after an engine failure. In West Germany the aircraft was described as a national scandal, with 252 accidents and 177 that have crashed. Also 24 have been lost in Italy. The current figures stand to be updated. Of the 1,900 manufactured, 600 have crashed. There is no doubt that this is an absolute tragedy. It is a serious situation. It is ridiculous for the Government to maintain aircraft with such a performance record.
Some of the rationalizations which have been used to justify continued usage of the aircraft are interesting. One article indicates that fighter pilots like to fly the CF-104, that it is a great honour, and that it is like the infantry soldier who knows there is risk but wants to be doing what he is doing. Unfortunately the five people who were killed on the highway in Germany did not want to happen what happened to them. Of the two persons who lost their lives in Alberta, one had a wife and four children. I am sure they do not want to be doing what they are doing today.
We in the House of Commons must ask ourselves whether this is justified. Frankly, in peacetime, astronomical losses of a dangerous aircraft such as that are completely intolerable.
Returning to the Cold Lake situation, the two aircraft that we lost did not appear to have been equipped with normal emergency locater equipment. The justification that military aircraft are exempt from carrying emergency locater transmitters is absolutely appalling on the part of the Canadian Government. Armed Forces pilots are probably the best trained and the most safety conscious pilots-beyond the shadow of a doubt. For the Canadian Government to permit the aircraft to be flown without ELTs is an extremely poor example to civilian pilots the Government is trying to convince should adhere to the law and maintain their aircraft. It is also a very poor example to set in respect of aviation safety. Unfortunately in cases of accidents where pilots survive in hostile countries, it could result their deaths. Emergency locater transmitters must be installed on all those aircraft. There must be operational changes in the aircraft. Unfortunately on the day that this matter was raised in the House the Minister indicated that there would be none and that the aircraft would continue to fly.
I submit that there must be a public investigation into the aircraft and its crashes, a search for common threads. The Minister made a commitment to make crash investigation records available indicating the variety and number of aircraft that went down, and the causes. I ask that he fulfil that commitment. The Minister must prohibit the use of those aircraft in aerial and aerobatic demonstrations. It is just too risky for the pilot to fly the aircraft at low levels, and it is too dangerous for the people watching.
Finally, the Minister must prohibit the use of the CF-104 in commercial airports. There can be no justification for flying this aircraft into heavily populated areas such as Vancouver

June 9, 1983
Adjournment Debate
and Winnipeg, where civilian airports are used. It is completely unjustifiable. The Minister must recognize that he cannot hide or attempt to justify these tragic accidents. We must all be very forthright and move quickly to investigate the causes. We must also act quickly to put the aircraft into very rigid operational roles in which they are known to be safe before we lose anymore pilots and before we have a repeat of the kind of tragedy we recently saw in Germany.

speakeroldname: Mr. Stanley Hudecki (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-REQUEST THAT CF-104 AIRCRAFT BE BANNED FROM AEROBATIC DEMONSTRATIONS. (B) REQUEST FOR DOCUMENTATION ON ACCIDENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member expresses several concerns in regard to the regrettable accident which occurred during an air display last month in Germany. He has questioned the operational suitability of the CF-104 in its current role in Europe, its accident record and also its continuing suitability for operations. The specific questions he has posed would take much longer to answer than the three minutes allotted to me. I will therefore just generalize and give him the highlights. Hopefully on a more personal basis and through correspondence I can give him the details.
On all of these contentions I must strongly take him to task, not only on the tone, the implications and indeed the facts that he has used in questioning the use of this aircraft, but especially on his lack of appreciation and sensitivity to the very difficult task that the pilots are called upon to perform for the security of this country. As the Minister has already pointed out in the House, we would not allow our pilots to take to the air in any aircraft if there were any questions whatsoever relating to the operational safety and soundness of the aircraft.
It has been accurately reported in the media that both the United States and the Canadian experience with this aircraft in so far as accidents rate are concerned is similar. Indeed, the same is true with regard to the accident rates of our six NATO allies who are also flying this aircraft in the European theatre. The CF-104 is a high performance military aircraft intended
for use in a very hostile environment. This inevitably requires specialized training missions that simulate actual wartime conditions.
This plane is not used for aerobatics at the various exhibits. It is simply a fly-past and the impression that is left on the spectators results from the speed at which they fly and the concomitant noise they produce.
With regard to the specifics of this unfortunate accident, may I assure the Hon. Member that, as with all accidents involving Canadian Forces aircraft, we are conducting an intensive investigation into the causes. May I assure the Hon. Member that the findings of these investigations are not secret, although some of the information gathered may indeed be of a confidential nature.
I can tell the Hon. Member that during the last five years only 13 per cent of the CF-104 accidents have been caused by identified material deficiencies. Therefore, to suggest that the aircraft is not airworthy for war service is simply not true. Our pilots are among the best trained pilots in the world. They are consummate professionals. They do not shy away from the CF-104. Indeed, they look forward to serving with it. They consider the opportunity to fly this high-performance aircraft in a demanding role a privilege. It is an extremely demanding job which they carry out with the utmost of professional capability, and we are rightly proud of them. I see my time is up, Mr. Speaker.
